item.title: In Search Of Gino Vannelli
item.dc:creator: ava
item.content:encoded:
Eyetalian Magazine, Winter 1997/1998

He was financially broken and suicidal after a sorid battle with his record company wiped out his gains of his early success in the seventies. Andrew Clark uncovers how singer Gino Vannelli reinvented himself, rediscovered his voice and why is ready to record again.

A snapshot: Gino Vannelli, 1974. His shirt a brilliant blue, as if he had been cut from a clear indigo Italian sky. It is open almost down to his navel. His jeans swell at the heel and grasp tightly around his hips. His hair cascades in a full mane of black locks. He leans forward on his left leg and stretches his right hand, which clasps a microphone, towards the heavens. Pelvis rocking like a metronome.

His visage is that of a fallen angel. Innocence toppled by desire. He is 21 and he is everything that the rest of the world’s 21 year olds want to be. Free. Confident. Romantic. Utterly and unabashedly consumed by his own ego. Gino is making his TV debut on America’s hippest show, Soul Train. The audience grooves to his moves and melodies. His song, “People Gotta Move” is a Top 20 hit and particularly popular with what A&R; executives call “the black market”.

The tune took him all of ten minutes to write. His girlfriend, in a flurry of rage, had chastised him for thinking an Italian kid from Montreal would make it in the music business. “You think it’s that easy”, she said. You think you’ll just go to Los Angeles and make records? “Yes. It was that easy. “I’ll bet you I can write a hit song right now.” He had, right there, and now he and his brothers Joe and Ross were playing it live for an American TV audience.

His dress and his attitude are Summer of Love. His voice is a throwback. A Raphaelite swoon steeped in a Byronesque obsession with the strange order of life. It is a cool seductive mix of choir boy exuberance and urban sixties agit prop.

Twenty years later only the voice would remain unchanged. In 1997, the mention of his name in media circles invokes comments like “Didn’t he change his name to Baron Longfellow” and “Didn’t he see the Devil?” The glowing Italian son has set into murky, curious myth.

Gino Vannelli was the first Italian Canadian to be what he was-a Gino. His music stood on its own merits: solid, at times inspired pop songs that were beautifully arranged and sung. Vannelli’s image gave Italians a chance to revel in their uniqueness. To not only like their night-black hair and olive skin but to accentuate them. To the Anglo mainstream he offered a chance to vicariously experience characteristics which its British heritage did not allow, like emotions. Vannelli, with his boiling passions, sincerity and brazen sexuality, was a release valve. In fact the popularity of Italian culture in the seventies hung mainly on its ability to placate an Anglo desire to unleash repressed demons.. AS ONE FAN HAS WRITTEN ON GINOV.COM, “HE SAID WHAT I DARED NOT SAY OR THINK”. Italy has always played this role. Shakespeare had used it as a setting for his most bloodiest and most treacherous tradgedies. Here was a Gino the mainstream would enjoy. He was a Romeo for all women to covet and Italian boys to emulate.

“A lot of my male friends really identified with Gino Vannelli,” says Gianna Patriarca, a poet who grew up during the seventies in Toronto’s Little Italy on College Street. “He was not only physically gorgeous, he was making a statement with his music. I remember my friend arguing that Gino Vannelli would be the most enduring musician of his generation.”

Vannelli was born in Montreal in 1952. His grandfather who landed in Canada at the turn of the century had started the “Roxy” chain of hair salons in the 1930. Gino’s father Russ Vannelli, was musically gifted. He was a noted singer for Montreal’s best big bands during the forties. A career in music, however, was out of the question. Gino’s grandfather expected all three of his sons to enter the hair salon business. sacrifices were made in order to ensure the prosperity of the family.

Gino’s talent was evident at a young age. By nine, he had procured his own set of bongos. He had been in a drug store with his father and snatched a pair of eight dollar drums from the shelf and immediately proceeded to bang on them, demonstrating considerable prowess. “If you don’t buy that kid those drums”, the pharmacist told Vannelli’s father, “I will”.

Young Gino sang in the church choir throughout elementary school and he was in love with the Catholic church. Vannelli would often attend two services on Sundays just to hear the organs and hymns. His home life was traditional: a close family unit with the accompanying claustrophobia. “It was both a heaven and a hell”, 47 year old Vannelli says from his home in Portland, Oregon where he is finishing a new CD which is due out in the Spring of 98. “There was lots to depend on and look forward to, at the same time everyone had their own aspirations to be different and assert themselves.”

Vannelli began playing in clubs at the age of 11. His greatest passion was the drums but, by age 15, he was beginning to discover the voice that would eventually make him a millionaire. He was also writing songs. It was around this time that Vannelli broke with the church. “A lot of of the Catholic church was based upon a threat. That’s a good way to make a child do something but its not a good way to lead a child into adulthood.”

He and his brothers Ross and Joe formed a band called the Jacksonville five. The Vannelli brothers managed a record deal with RCA. At age 16, Gino recorded under the name Van Elli. He thought Vannelli was too ethnic. The single became a top it in Canada. After a stint in New York City, Gino decided it was time to try the West Coast.

The Vannelli brothers hit Los Angeles in 1972. One of Gino’s friends sent the group’s demo tapes around the major studios but they pulled little interest. Money ran out quickly. His parents had wired money but that had sent it to the wrong Hollywood (Hollywood, Florida). The boy wonder singer was faced with the prospect of returning to Montreal without a deal.

On the morning they were set to fly out, Gino rose early and took off down Sunset( back then people still walked in L.A.). He found a church and slipped in for a few moments’ quiet. He had a vision, he says, of “waiting by the gates.” Vannelli went back to the hotel and told his brother Joe, “I can’t tell you where I’m going but if you want to follow, you’ll follow.”

Gino went to the office of A&M; records at 10:00 a.m., his goal, to way-lay record big shot Herb Alpert. Finally, at about 2 p.m. Alpert appeared. Vannelli recalls, “I said, Joe, hold my guitar’, and ran right through the gates. The guards were chasing me. Herb freaked out. He was shaky. In the last year or two he had received kidnap threats. I told him, ‘I want to play for you.’ After he realized I wasn’t a terrorist, he listened. He told me to come back in half an hour .”

Vannelli left that afternoon with an A&M; record deal.. Vannelli’s ascent began. During the remainder of the seventies his music rose up the charts. His first album, Crazy Life, did not do well. Vannelli went on the road opening for Stevie Wonder. His albums Powerful People, Storm at Sunup, Gist of the Gemini, and Pauper in Paradise sold about 500,000 each. Vannelli toured constantly, building his audiences from nightclub crowds of 300 to arena mobs. The singer was on the road so much that he had no permanent home. His convoy included 41 staff and 4 semi trailers to haul the 17 synthesizers and instruments from town to town.

Vannelli became famous for his lush, highly synthesized orchestral melodies that were mixed with funk percussions. He was also known for his poster boy looks and was picked as Hunk of the Month by Sixteen magazine. He remained an oddity. An Italian in the rock and roll business.

“Many times I felt the predjudice. There was this image that Italians aren’t important in contemporary music. Truly, there hasn’t been that many Italians who have pierced the Anglo-fied culture. Italians don’t feel the same way, they’re really more romantically inclined.”

By 1977, Vannelli was feeling the pressure both from his record label and from his family to make a commercial record. These forces ran contrary to Vannelli’s instinct. He had been more intrigued by writing more orchestral works and had recorded The Pauper in Paradise album with the London Philharmonic. He relented and the result was the 1978 Brother to Brother album which featured the song I Just Wanna Stop, a tune written by Ross Vannelli, on which Gino polished the lyrics.

The Brother to Brother album sold approximately two million copies. Vannelli was nominated for a Grammy award for best singer. Industry giant Arista records offered him a lucrative deal and he signed. Vannelli says they courted him sweetly. They said everything that a self-absorbed artist wants to hear. He released the Nightwalker album in 1981, after marrying in 1980, Vannelli stopped touring and wouldn’t tour again until 1991. Like it’s predecessor, The Nightwalker had a hit, the lonesome ballad, “Living Inside Myself”. It too won a Grammy nomination. Vannelli continued to rise. He went into the studio and recorded an album. Arista records heard it and loathed it. Almost immediately relations went sour. All his years of work blew away like dust. Vannelli found himself at war with his own label.

The quarrel was simple: Vannelli was accustomed to a large measure of license. Arista was accustomed to a large measure of control. Arista records wanted Gino to sing the songs Arista Records dictated. Vannelli learned that his contract, which he thought protected him, left him a puppet. It appeared that he could release no work, not a note, without Arista’s approval. A four year struggle ensued. The fighting became so petty that the song Living Inside Myself was banned from the Arista Christmas party. For a period Vannelli became partially dependant on anti-depressants.

“I was willing to bend a bit but it was what they wanted me to record. They wanted me to record “Even the Nights Are Better” I think one of the worst songs ever written. I said, ‘You don’t understand, I can’t sing a song like that.’ Then, after Air Supply recorded the song, and it was number one, I received a call and the voice said: ‘See I told you so’. I said, ‘What are you telling me? The fact that it’s number one bears no significance on my life. They were confounded.

“My career was going to die. I couldn’t do anything. Everybody thought my career had peaked at age 27. I couldn’t get any other record company to buy out my deal.

Eventually he gave Arista what they wanted- everything he had. Vannelli bought out his contract. Against the wishes of some family members he purchased his freedom. The move cost him all the money he had amassed during his career. He also signed away earnings from future records.

Vannelli bottomed out. He immediately started work on a new album. Vannelli recorded the Black Cars album in his brother Joe’s home studio and signed with Dreyfuss Records, using the money to pay off his Arista debts. Vannelli also hired a new manager. “He commanded me to cut my hair. He groomed me. I hated it. Then I realized he was right. It was all part of smashing my image.”

Thus faded the picture of the romantic seventies singer. The original Gino was gone. He was replaced by the eighties. Slick suits. Hip swivels. Music videos. The good looks still intact, Black Cars which was released in 1985, proved to be Vannelli’s most commercially successful, winning sales in Europe and Canada. The Montreal heartthrob had bounced back, at least materially. Spiritually, he was in a state of permanent dusk. Vannelli teetered between day and night, between life and death.

“Everything I had built myself up to be was really truly an illusion that I’d built up in my head,” he admits. “I had too many unanswered questions. I couldn’t write anymore. I had nothing to say anymore. I couldn’t feel anything at the piano. I couldn’t feel my voice. I couldn’t hear my voice. I couldn’t stand my voice. I couldn’t stand the idea of show business. I was a breadth away from saying goodbye to the world.”

Over the next five years Vannelli embarked on an odyssey. He became keenly interested in the occult and in various forms of religion, everything from Buddhism to the Cabbala. Vannelli flew to Japan and spent time in a Buddhist monastery. He went to Peru and spoke with shamans. In Europe, he visited with monks. One monk suggested that before he search for a crashing experience with God, that he should “get an accountant.”

Vannelli dedicated himself to becoming a voracious reader and consumed, by his estimation, between 500 and 1000 books on philosophy and religion. He practiced martial arts and meditation. Eventually, these pursuits led to a series of what he describes as “mind shattering, ego shattering, revelatory experiences.”

Journalist Peter Howell, who in 1991 was the Toronto Star’s pop critic, recalls interviewing Vannelli after one such experience: “He practically started talking in tongues. He went into this weird spiritual trip. He said he had lost all his ego and turned himself into a spiritual force…I thought he was close to being unhinged. I felt like I was this guy’s shrink. He was saying things that were really intense. It wasn’t an agenda. He was letting it pour out.”

Howell’s attitude was indicative of the overall attitude the media took towards Vannelli’s spiritual turn. On a certain level it was to be expected. Artists, be they musicians, poets, or actors, who adopt a spiritual tone are regularly castigated. There may be, however, a little more at work in the case of Gino Vannelli. The critics and public had accepted his first incarnation-the love tossed balladeer. Likewise, they had embraced his eighties Armani posturing. His follow-up to Black Cars, Big Dreamers Never Sleep had also been a success. Theses were Gino. A pondering spiritual crusader, such as the one who appeared on the 1991 Inconsolable man CD, was one step too far. His 1995 album, Yonder Tree, was a commercial bust.

“I think the critics were totally unfair.” says Vancouver-based CKLG disc jockey Stu Jeffries, formerly the host of CBC television’s Good Rockin’ Tonight. “They were not willing to let go of the Gino Vannelli everybody knew. He has a lot more to offer and has accomplished far more, even in the seventies, than bands are trying to accomplish in the nineties.”

This creative roadblock is significant when you consider that no other entertainer has exemplified the Italian experience in Canada as fully as Gino Vannelli. He came of age in the early seventies, just as the second and third generations of Italy’s immigrant children were clumsily making their way between two worlds, the old and the new. Prior to Vannelli, there had been Italian celebrities, all of them American. They offered old school images. They were either boxers like Rocky Marciano or singers like Fabian, who tried to wash their Italian genes from their music and looks. Only Frank Sinatra did not hide his Italian roots. These boy-toy singers made out like Italian WASPs. Like many Italian Canadians, Vannelli considers his heritage an act of chance, a part of his overall being, but not its defining characteristic. He considers himself an individual and an artist first. When Vannelli expressed these beliefs, and his spiritual ponderings, in the Yonder Tree album, he came under fire. When he ceased to fit the Gino image he was whacked.

Whether or not he is capable of translating his spiritual awakenings into music is immaterial. Regardless of the quality of Vannelli’s philosophical musings it is important to note that he was chastised for making the attempt. He was criticized first and foremost because he had the temerity to try, and to try it, not in a fringe art such as literature, but in a mainstream medium. It was as if he had strayed out of bounds. Romance and passion worked. They were Italian domains. Philosophical musings? No, no.

Italian Canadians who care about their place in society should take note….(the next few paragraphs of this article go on to admonish Italians to break into areas that do not fit the Italian stereotype)

……As for Gino Vannelli, he has reached a happy medium. His new CD, with the working title Faith, Hope, and a Dash of Despair is more commercial than his last but has the artistic weight he requires. Will it click with listeners? If Vannelli has proven anything, it’s that he has a talent for weathering storms, both external and of his own making.

There’s a good chance he will find popular success once again. More importantly, he says, he has found the sunny peace he searched continents to unearth. In many ways it is ironically reminiscent of the morals he heard preached from the pulpit.

“I have a son to raise and a wife to love,” he says. “My sweetest revenge is that I’m going on and making my music and that I have found a good life.

“I am willing to live by the code of polaric rules that are part of human existence. Instead of trying to be like Jesus Christ and control the waves, I’ll ride the waves.”
item.excerpt:encoded: An essay about Gino Vannelli as published in the Winter 1997/98 issue of Eyetalian Magazine

item.title: Finding Peace in the Valleys of Valhalla
item.dc:creator: ava
item.content:encoded:
By Carnell
Carpre Noctem™ Magazine,
Volume III, Issue 2, December 1996

One of the nice things about running your own magazine is that you get to talk with people you hold in the highest regard. I was seventeen when I first heard of Gino Vannelli and was totally unprepared for the depth of intelligence carved into the grooves of the record. A hallmark of Gino’s music is the effortless use of intelligent lyricism and a master’s sense of melody. An amalgam of jazz, pop, classical and R&B;, it possesses the depth of any Hegelian dialectic and the lyrical elegance of a Shakespearean sonnet. His songs speak of man searching for some glimmer of the Eternal Truths we all look for: love, understanding and coming to terms with who we are and what we stand for. His music is at once accessible and technically proficient. On albums such as Gist of the Gemini, A Pauper in Paradise, Brother to Brother, Nightwalker, Inconsolable Man and the latest release, Yonder Tree, Gino has spanned genres and broken molds. Gino Vannelli’s music is probably not something you are used to hearing, but once heard, it is something to which you will find yourself continually drawn.

Who am I
To the rabble and the wise;
Am I just a young and shallow face;
That years erase;
Am I more than that;
Do they wonder?
How can I;
Bring the world beneath this guise;
In the silence of my languished soul;
Lies a truth unknown;
Yes, I am. I am just an ugly man
Alone.
– “Ugly Man” Gist of the Gemin

When you were growing up, what was some of the music you were listening to and what influenced you the most?

A series. Many styles of music. My father was a jazz and big band aficionado. Of course, we grew up with all of the pop music that everybody else grew up with. I myself enjoyed classical music very well and would try to attend as many school concerts or school sponsored concerts from the Montreal Symphony as I could. So, I would say that the elements of pop, jazz and classical were very strong with me.

Were you a part of the organized school band?

Oh yeah, I used to sing in the Glee Club. I used to always give concerts for classmates and what not, there was always something going on.

What about now? What are you hearing that excites you?

There’s always something that excites me. It could be the song itself, the lyric, maybe the drum sound, or maybe someone’s playing ability, maybe some singer’s great voice. I mean I heard an old Ella tape the other day that was just killer. Who knows? It could be anything, but there are certainly plenty of classic works and classic composers and singers to get excited about still.

Stand by the window
Close to the edge
As the neon signs surrender to the light of day
I sip a bitter cup of coffee
and I fade away oh I fade away
There’s a cross above my pillow
Curse words on the wall
What I’d give to write the pages of my life again
No, I can’t believe this is the way
The story ends.
Oh is this the end?
Is this the end? I wanna run to the highest mountain
I wanna stand in the light of the sun
I wanna ask all this world to forgive
The man that I’ve become
And now I call on the angels above
Won’t somebody hear won’t somebody hear
My cry of love.
– “Cry of Love” Inconsolable Man

I know early on when you started to have hits with “I Just Wanna Stop,” you were pigeon-holed into this “Canadian sex symbol” thing. Was that a difficult thing for you to shed?

Difficult from the stand point that people have a very narrow perspective of what it was and what I did. I think that clouded their vision, not that most people who thought that of me really had any good vision to begin with, because anybody who could hear anything would know that was something that was a misnomer or a misconception of me.

Was it something that, as soon as it started to happen, you tried to do damage control early on and tried to present as much of the real you as possible?

The thing that is confusing is if an artist is fighting just for recognition anyway-because recognition means you get to keep doing what you’re doing and so, if you sell enough records you can make another record. It means you are artistically happy and you can eat. So, part of the whole scheme and plan of trying to make an artist successful is to try to bring as many attributes as he has out to the fore. And so, obviously, at one point, I’d wear my hair a certain way and wear certain clothes that I was just comfortable with and so, if a picture was taken that happened to look a little sexy or something like that and anyone from the record company or managers would say, “Well, that’s a good picture. I think that’s sellable.” All of a sudden you find that a million people think you are a certain way that you are not. So, things happen awfully slowly in this business and sometimes they happen overnight. Things like that are really difficult to shed because people tend to think that anybody with any kind of physical attribute had to be empty-headed or lame-brained. The theory is disproven day in and day out.

I know artists like Mariah Carey run into that. People think, “Ah, she’s just a look.”

I don’t think Mariah has anything to worry about. [laughs]

You were once quoted as saying, “My music comes from a search for something that’s different in myself.” Can you explain a little about that?

Well, the search for something different is really the search itself, because if you were searching for the same thing, you wouldn’t be searching, right? As years have gone by I’ve realized I’ve been one who enjoys the search. Sometimes, the search is very painful, but always there is a short end to the search. There always is an end to the chapter and then the book keeps going. The search itself is the search for the perfect chord, the perfect word, the perfect title, the perfect vocal, the perfect meaning, the search for the perfect person to be your friend, or the search for the perfect vision of God.

There’s no time to wallow in my cheer
‘Tis mine to make my life a better place for my song;
Near my blues will be gone;
Bracing my joy till June.
– “There’s No Time” Crazy Life

At a time when you are compelled by a deadline to deliver a product, are you ever completely satisfied? Do you ever walk away from a song and say, “That was perfect. Everything was where it should be?”

Sometimes. I do have that excitement level and sometimes I’ll tend to over-do it and try to make it more than it should have been. It’s a really hard thing to judge. Usually, I push it until it pushes me back. That’s when I get to hate it a little bit, but then I know once I get to that point-it’s done.

You were also quoted as having said, “My one objective is to be respected and successful.” Is this still a major concern for you?

I must have been twenty-one when I said that.[laughs]

It was 1979.

Yeah… that’s a typical twenty-five year old statement. You want to feel power, yet you want to feel loved. I suppose those are nice things to have, but over the years, my continuous and most obsessive objective is just to do my best and to do work that really pleases me.

Where am I going?
Have I gone too far?
Have I lost my mind?
Where are my eyes?
Oh, have I seen too much?
Have I lost my touch?
Losing directions from growing infections;
Poisoned desires of reaping life so young.
“Where Am I Going” Storm at Sunup

One of the themes I see a lot in your music is that of a man coming to terms with who he is and what he is all about. Are the songs, then, reflections of your own search?

Well, you know how the Actor’s Studio touted their Method Acting, where the actor would become that person and the skill was the immersion and the actor would be the tentacle of this mind? With me, much of what I record-what I say lyrically-is sort of that Method Acting or Method Singing or Method Writing. When I really do become that theme and I really feel it in my body and I feel it on my skin. I’m not one of those singers or composers who can really write a skillful love song out of the blue.

More and more
Your kiss is like a half opened door
I can’t get in
You stop me just before I begin
And it hurts to be in love
When you never get enough
Oh, it hurts to be in love
This endless urge
Keeps my body right on the verge
We touch and then
I want to do it over again.
– “It Hurts To Be In Love” Black Cars

One of the things I like about your writing is that, even in songs where the theme is as simple as love-if love can be simple-you manage to, with a turn of a lyric, make it an extremely personal statement.

I think that’s where the power is. The power universal is in the personal. The universal love song is only really powerful when it shrinks down to the size of a head of a needle. Then, you can really see it, you can touch it.

During the 80’s you went on a “spiritual pilgrimage.” What was the cause of that? Was it something that you felt you needed to do, or were you searching for something bigger than yourself?

Well, you know, outer space is bigger than myself. Inner space is deeper than myself. I was expanding and contracting as much as I could. In order to really expand, you have to really go deeper. Simple observations were necessary because my life started to become ruled by the effects of the market place on my career. And then, when I wasn’t as successful as I wanted to be, my life was falling apart, and I needed some things to be attended to, problems, growing up problems that I really hadn’t faced until I reached thirty. I found myself incapable of expanding. It took me ten years to just realize, staring at a tree that its roots needed to be in deep as its head was high. So, I could not expand, have these visions of expanding my personal influence in music unless I knew myself better, unless I went deeper and dug my roots deeper. It became the search. The search for feeling. The search that I was always doing, but very unconscious of it. Then it became an all out search where it wasn’t just something I was going to write about in a song. It became a “do-or-die,” “all bets are off,” “we need to find out what the truth is.”

What role did your family play in that?

Sometimes a balancing role, just to remember how I was just a kid born on a certain city block, played on swings and played in the band, and all of that. Sometimes, very inhibiting, very limiting, very condescending, disbelieving, skeptical. And at times, like I said, very grounding.

You have described your outlook as that of a “Zen theosophist.” Can you elaborate on that?

Theosophy is really a culmination of all of the occult arts. Zen, at its heart, is really an occult practice, although it doesn’t have the academia that theosophy has. It’s academia on the experiential side. Zen theosophy might as well be any kind of theosophy. Theosophy really comprises, at its best, all of these elements. Zen is a particular color of experience, of perspective, very dry, very transistorized. It’s as the crow flies to the truth. It’s unembellished. It’s not like Tibetan Buddhism. You sit down and you scratch everything away until you’re clear. It’s not really based on ritual and trying to get a feeling through emotion. It’s Karate versus Tai Chi. Tai Chi is a dance and Zen is the spearhead aiming for the bull’s-eye. Theosophy is the study of it, the understanding of it. It is much more intellectually based than Zen is. It’s very Westernized, but it’s very good, because here in our Western society, we need to get to our intellect because we have very developed intellects. We ask a lot of questions like, “Why? What’s in it for me? What’s it gonna really do?” So, when you ask those kind of questions, you need theosophy or some occult art as that like Jewish Kabbala to really answer a lot of those nagging intellectual questions that you do have, to get you to the place where you can trust and go into the experience.

You have a unique ability to draw some of the top musicians to play with you. Is that a conscious thing where you say, “To perform my music to the level of which I want it performed, I have to pull in the likes of Dave Garibaldi, Jimmy Haslip and Vinnie Coliauta.”?

Yeah, that’s really what it comes down to. I’m doing three or four more R&B; based songs on this new album that I’m recording right now. I’m doing them with Brian McKnight and I can say Brian McKnight’s the best artist at what he does. He has influence with his R&B; abilities, his singing ability and I don’t really think I could make this come off without Brian’s help. It’s a question of you realizing what you need, you need someone to be able to fulfill those needs. It’s as simple as it is.

So, R&B; is a direction that you will continue to pursue…

You know, there is a funk R&B; perspective that I’d like to put on this new album here. There’s always a jazz perspective that I love and Brian’s got a lot of those influences so it’s really fun working with him because we can get something different. I can be influenced by someone very different than who I am and it brings a whole different element to what I do…the theory of getting a good producer to help you. [laughs]

Do you consider the more “rock” based music we saw you doing on albums like Nightwalker and Inconsolable Man a chapter closed?

Well, no, because I don’t think that album’s going to be all that way. The R&B; cuts that are going to be on this album will be more geared towards radio, I suppose, and they’re really good songs. There are a lot of other songs on the album that are not just geared that way. I do have my nine minute piece with this album. [laughs] I just spent the whole day orchestrating it with a piano player. It’s quite involved. It’s called “Heaven Denied.” It’s actually the story of Beethoven.

It’s so funny, I just watched Immortal Beloved not more than a couple of days ago…

I’ve always been a fan of Beethoven and that movie-I saw it three or four times-all of a sudden, this whole melody and this whole theme came to me. The whole theme of “Heaven Denied” is basically, “Why can’t I hear you?”

I’m glad you brought up film. Based on your orchestral work on Pauper in Paradise, have you ever considered scoring a film?

It’s never raised its pretty little head. I’ve always been busy taking care of my career and doing what not. I started to have some calls. In fact, [there] was a call from a producer a couple of months ago and I was going to give him a song that was quite classical in orientation to help develop the whole theme of the movie around it. I found out that they had drug money involved. The whole thing fell apart. The whole twelve million of their budget just collapsed on them because the guy went to jail. So much for my movie career. [laughs]

As I was preparing for this interview, I was listening to some of the Pauper in Paradise album and that piece in particular just screams for a film.

The Oregon Symphony has asked me to perform it live with them and so, we’re going to start there. I’ll just fix up a few parts and re-orchestrate a few things and update it. I’d like to do that. I’ve written another piece, too. It’s an hour and a half piece; it’s more like an opera. I’ll record it after this coming album.

So, you’ll commit it to laminate. It used to be vinyl, now I guess it’s something else.

You know I will, definitely.

Looking at your albums, Yonder Tree and Inconsolable Man, there is such a big break. Was this a desire to get into a more jazz-based kind of music?

Yeah, I’ve always loved jazz especially fifties-influenced jazz. I wanted to do an album that had that kind of bass to it. Shall I kiss the mouth, stroke the hair;
Undress her – do I dare
Or bite into the vein above her heaving breast
Ah, the sun best come up soon
There’s no telling with the moon over madness.
– “Moon Over Madness” Yonder Tree

As the album progresses, it starts very “smoky room” sort of jazz flavor and then about two thirds of the way through, culminating with “Moon Over Madness”, it’s such a range that you almost see the range without noticing it.

I know what you’re saying. “Moon Over Madness” is just one of those things where I struggled with the notion that it may have not been applicable to the album, but I just thought that the idea was so urgent that I had to put it on.

It’s a great tune.

It really is. I enjoy it, too. It took a lot to personify the [character], but what convinced me to do it is that I have such a keen perspective on why Bram Stoker wrote it that I figured I had to really express this perspective as a man who is really torn and finally meeting someone that he falls in love with and he realized that he’s just about to enlighten himself to love. Part of him realizes that if he does enlighten himself and draw himself to her love, that it is the end of him. Someone’s gotta die.

It reminded me of the Louis character from Anne Rice’s book.

A little bit. There has to be that. When you get a character that becomes sociopathic, to me, they’re terribly boring.

It’s that conflict.

Conflict is nothing more than polarity. Polarity is, like I say, the tree struggling to make it to the sun and yet its roots struggle to go deeper into the earth and the tension is beautiful. It makes music. That’s what great music is all about, controlled tension.

You are doing some producing of other artists, such as Gianni Bella, Kudasai, and David Meece.

[Gianni Bella is] an Italian guy. I just did a duet with him. Do you have that record?

No.

It’s very good.

Well, you’re preaching to the choir on this one. I can’t imagine a recording coming from you that wouldn’t be good. Is that a direction you want to continue?

No. I really want to be an artist and continue to write. That’s more of what I want to do, but sometimes a friend comes along, or someone from another country who just offers me a gargantuan amount of money to sit down. I go, “Well, ok, if that’s what you want to do.” And if the record is good, the song is good, the people are right and all of those elements come into play, I say, “Well all right. Let’s do it.”

I really liked the two pieces you did on David Meece’s greatest hits CD.

What was that? Oh, “Come that Day” and “Seventy Times Seven.”

The funny thing was, as I listened to the rest of that album, when you get to those tracks, even though he may be singing, you can see your thumb print firmly over the whole track.

Well, sometimes I run into problems with that. “I’m not you” and I say, “I’m sorry, I got a vision.”

Have you ever considered doing a more ambient sounding recording?

No, my tendency is more toward intensified communication.

Which of your recordings do you think comes the closest to who Gino truly is?

I don’t know. I’d have to pigeon-hole myself. I love “A Little Bit of Judas” a lot, but I also like “Pauper in Paradise.” I think there are some cuts on Nightwalker that are really good. I really couldn’t say. They’re all facets of my personality.

I’ve seen highways in the rain
Waved good-bye to midnight trains
I seen sweet dreams disappear
All my life
I felt cold wind cut my skin
Waiting on ships that never came in
But I’ve never cried real tears until tonight.
– If I Should Lose This Love” Inconsolable Man

After Nightwalker came out, there was talk of an album called Twisted Heart. What ever happened to that?

Oh, it got shelved in battles with the record company. It was a terribly long battle much like George Michael’s battle and it was terrible for me. I couldn’t record for four or five years and it really hurt me.

What happened to all of the material?

It’s just on a shelf and I’m just on to a whole other thing. Someday, I suppose I’ll release it just for comedy’s sake. [laughs]

I know so many people who want to see you perform live. Will you be doing any touring in the near future?

I just got off a tour seven or eight months ago. I did an extensive tour of the states, twenty three or twenty four nights and twenty two nights in Europe, twelve nights in Japan, five nights in Canada.

Have you ever played the San Francisco Bay Area?

I have not.

It’s funny. I was in Los Angeles a few years ago and I had just missed you playing by a day.

I played the House of Blues there.

That was it. That was the gig.

It was pretty good.

[laughs] Thanks. “Here’s some salt for your wound.”

I had a really good band. Really good.

He’s just rubbing it in.

It was more of a jazz-oriented band and we took a lot of the old material and revamped it, jazzified it, stretched it out. It was interesting.

Tonight I watch you in your sleep;
Wondering what dark secrets you keep
Away from me
A careless word falls from your lips
A time and place that somehow slips
From a memory
I feel my way through darkness
But I trust in where your heart is.
– Something Tells Me” Big Dreamers Never Sleep

I loved what you did to “Something Tells Me” on the live album.

Oh that. It’s one of my better songs.

So, you’re doing the new album and then, once that’s completed you’ll probably tour again.

No, not readily. I’ve got some other things that I really want to get done. I really need to finish this hour and a half symphonic opera that I’m working on. So, I don’t think I’ll get out until six months after the release of the album. I suppose, at some point, I will.

What is the new album called?

Geez, I don’t know yet. I’m just in the stages now where all of the material is written. I have maybe three songs left to write lyrics to and we’re starting to produce it within a month. I’d like to get it done for Christmas.

I work no day with self deception;
All that I am is one common grain of sand;
But the sun does rise for every man alive
And now my heart is clear
Cause I have from what I do
And I do just what I am.
O no man is born a starless sky
‘Neath his naked hide
Lord yes I am, maybe I’m a lucky man
Inside
– “Ugly Man” Gist of the Gemini
item.excerpt:encoded: An interview with Gino Vannelli from the December 1996 issue of Carpe Noctem Magazine

item.title: A New Spiritualism Guides Gino Vannelli
item.dc:creator: ava
item.content:encoded:
Gary Graff, Detroit Journal Music Writer
October 6th, 1995

Gino Vannelli has pulled into Atlanta on a particularly eventful day.

The Atlanta Braves are preparing for their first game of the baseball playoffs (they won). But this excitement didn’t touch Vannelli. “You know,” he says, “I was just too busy. Everybody knew where the deliberations were at, but that was about it.” Ah yes, the deliberations. The O.J. Simpson trial. The verdict. How did Vannelli view all that? “I don’t know,” he offers. “Nobody is ever really going to know for sure. No matter what I say or you say, we weren’t there. All I can say is I wouldn’t want to be him right now.”

Actually, Vannelli is perfectly happy being himself these days. And it’s not quite the same Gino Vannelli you might remember from the ’70s — he of the bared, hair-covered chest belting out love songs over a dense backdrop of synthesizers. Vannelli has in recent years found God. And Buddah. And a new musical direction. As he puts it in on song from his new album, “Yonder Tree,” Vannelli has found “Jehovah and All that Jazz.”

“I do not believe in any one direction,” Vannelli, 43, says of the intensive spiritual search he began during the late ’70s. “All directions finally converge if you’re far enough down the line. I believe myself to be at a point where I know clearly the challenge of bringing a more spiritual consciousness into my dense brain here. “Whether it’s religion or philosophy or whatever, it’s like peeling onions; you do one layer at a time. If you try to pierce it, you’re not going to make it. It will be too rich or too pungent. You’ll literally blow up.”

It was, in fact, a kind of personal implosion that sent Vannelli scrambling for some meaning beyond music. The Montreal native claimed a niche in the ’70s pop pastiche with his lushly orchestrated — bombastic, even — hits such as “People Gotta Move” and 1978’s massive “I Just Wanna Stop.” Vannelli, it turns out, did want to stop around that time. Even though he had a few hits in the ’80s — “Living Inside Myself,” “Black Cars,” “Wild Horses” — he found himself spiritually adrift, satisfied with neither money nor fame. So he embarked on a study of what his manager, John Baruck, in the Wall Street Journal, called “the wisdom of the ages.”

Vannelli studied religion, philosophy and poetry. He spoke with Zen priests in Japan and Benedictine monks in California and Inca priests in Peru. He explored Christianity, Hinduism, Taoism, Nietzsche, Plato, Aristotle, Kant and the Kabbalah. These days Vannelli subscribes to no one school of thought but considers himself “a Zen theosophist.” He’s simplified his life, too, driving a Honda Accord and living comfortably but modestly in Portland, Ore., with his wife and 9-year-old son.

Vannelli says he always sensed his spiritual exploration would channel itself into music, but he didn’t rush it. Twenty years ago, he says, “I had these notions, lofty notions about life and wanting to employ them artistically. But I didn’t have the skills I possess now. I suppose I didn’t have the wherewithal that 20 years of searching has given me. “But to clearly state what I feel about these topics, when you’re talking about Jehovah or Judas or falling in love with reference to the great philosophers, you have to really have a grasp of what you’re saying and not just drop names.” Vannelli brought them all to “Yonder Tree,” but he also arrived with a different sound. The synthesizers are gone; now he sings in front of an acoustic jazz group, displaying a restraint that seemed unimaginable when he first began putting out albums. “It’s not terribly unlike some of the records I made in the ’70s,” he claims. “If you listen to ‘Storm at Sunup’ or ‘Gist of the Gemini’ . . . you know such an artist could probably do such a thing.”

But, he acknowledges, “Yonder Tree” does represent “a conscious effort to break the mold and not do something as commercial as ‘Black Cars’ or ‘Big Dreamers’ or the ‘Inconsolable Man’ album. It was a conscious effort to do something more progressive, more harmonically challenging — and stretching out lyrically into thoughts I dare not have spoken about before I was sure of my heart.” Vannelli thinks the music will be pouring out of him in the near future; he talks about another new album as soon as late summer. “I have a lot of ideas,” he says. “I’m still enamored with harmony and a jazzier sound.” And he hasn’t abandoned any of the old hits, either. He’s simply reworked them: “Living Inside Myself” has a chamberish, “Brahms-like” arrangement; while “Black Cars” sounds “like Coltrane coming together with a funk band.” “You know,” Vannelli says, “it suddenly dawned on me when I started the tour that the audience might be pissed off by that. But so far they’re not at all. They’re really enthused with the new arrangements.”

item.title: Yonder Tree – Song By Song
item.dc:creator: ava
item.content:encoded:
October 1995

Walter Whitman (Where Are You)

“Musically, I grew up with the jazz artists of the ’40s, ’50s, ’60s, all the singers from Billie Holiday, Billy Eckstein to Frank Sinatra, Tony Bennett, Joe Williams, Sarah Vaughan, Ella Fitzgerald. My father turned me on to all those singers… jazz has always been touted as being uncommercial, won’t sell anything, but then Harry Connick Jr. came along and repopularized it. But I didn’t want to make a Harry Connick album, or a Natalie Cole album. I wanted to make something in that genre, but not a collection of old songs — it would be difficult to be inspired.

“Walter Whitman had touched something I was yearning to touch and that was a little more affinity and loving toward myself. If I must follow a form, let the form carry me, but if I have to be constricted, then I die. Whitman could not be constricted by form, he knew where philosophy, where religion, where politics should begin and end.”

Fallen In Love

“I thought, `I’d kinda like a drum solo in this song, but then again, no.’ Something about that track reminded me of a ’30s, ’40s Fred Astaire thing, who better to get than Gregory Hines? I don’t know him, I just got his phone number from his agent. I sent him the track, he liked it instantly, said he was going to be in L.A. So I went down with my brother Joe, we build him a stage out of two 4×8 sheets of plywood we nailed together, put a bit of sand on it, Greg walked in with his tap shoes and said `let’s go!’

“Lyrically, it starts out as a Cole Porter kind of thing, but then it gets into what I was pursuing. All the great minds chase the answers, but you have to ask of them: `dammit, if you’re so smart, how come you’re so unhappy?’ And that was the whole song: for a moment of love I’d give it all away.”

You Owe It To Yourself

“Sometimes people separate, go different ways, lead different lives, different passions and they just find themselves apart. I looked at my wife and wondered if she’d ever come to me someday and say `I need to do this, need to feel that way,’ like, `my life is too much around you and your career,’ which I’ve always felt a little guilty of. Could I turn around and tell her she’s free to experience what she needs to experience? Could I be big enough to absorb the pain?”

A Little Bit Of Judas

“An ode to my fourth-grade catechism teacher… It’s very liberating to be able to take potshots at your belief system without fear you’re going to be struck by a lightning bolt. It’s about taking the sacred names, places, personal places, sacred sites, sacred feelings and saying `hey, it’s all up for grabs!’ You can do this, that… not only is there Judas in us all, but one should be able to take these names out of a hat and say them without a qualm.”

Unbearably Blue

“Can’t help but have eyes and ears and see and feel… the tension is always there. The tension to want to stray, to let your magnetic impulses take over… “Unbearably Blue” does its best to leave no trace of a clean answer to such unsolvable mysteries.”

Jehovah and All That Jazz

“The lyrics needed an appropriate, fun track to showcase them… Many of the great artists, Charlie Parker, John Coltrane, John Lennon, Jimi Hendrix, and so on were highly intolerable demons to upright society, but they certainly infused that same society with life. What we attribute the works of the devil to is what gives God life. There’s nothing more touted in a Christian bookstore than Satan: how to deal with him. At some point you say: `I’m tired of that drama and I prefer another one. It’s becoming awfully myopic, it’s really hurting more than it’s helping and this is why people are giving up the whole thing. ‘ John Coltrane was a very troubled person and even felt personally that he was possessed by demons. It’s that wild energy, that crazy fool inside us that wants to be let loose and play. Without it there’s nothing to harness. The devil is that bucking bronco, and if there’s no-one to ride it, there is no drama.”

None So Beautiful

“I have deep feelings toward people who give of themselves, that are unnoticed, unsung heroes. I don’t know their names, I don’t know who they are, but I wish to suffer with them.”

I Die A Little More Each Day

“There were moments of great joy and great sorrow experienced in the making of this album. I didn’t know how to express my sorrow, I didn’t just want to say `I hate the world’ for what’s happening to it. I tried to find a way to express that sorrow in a beautiful sense. It comes from a sense of empathy, a sense of sympathy, fear, outrage that we’re taking something so wonderful for granted. We devour our host, thinking there’s a heaven somewhere else, but it’s not true. The kingdom has been given to us and we’re to experience it; not subdue it, conquer it, and deface it… the sudden realization that our mother called Earth is being raped makes me cry, it also makes me die, because my body and my nourishment comes from this mother. To see her in such a state simply hurts. I don’t know any other way to say it. The hurt is doubly painful because the finger is pointed at myself first.”

Come To The Well

“It’s about the sacredness of sex. I was always taught to despise my passions, my lust, to look very suspiciously on it. My lust is part of my creativity, my desire to live; what I do with it is quite another matter. That sacredness is a phenonemal gift. When sexuality is killed, or kept alive by pornographers, by those who imagine it to be deviant and who therefore treat it as deviant, when you can only find it in deviant places and buy it from deviant sources it makes it a dirty thing. The physical expression of love is sexuality, the spiritual expression of sexuality is love. They go hand in hand.”

Moon Over Madness

“The drama of feeling your heart, passion and reacting to your basic impulses, which in this case is hostility, is one of the great horrors and conflicts to be experienced; without which, there is no drama, in fact no life at all. I believe the enlightenment of this vampire first begins with his confrontation with his own dilemma. The struggle that follows is for the observer to be witness to, and be entertained by.
item.excerpt:encoded: Gino Vannelli gives a song by song analysis of Yonder Tree, October 1995

item.title: Meditations Of A Monk Add Up To Assignment For An Accountant
item.dc:creator: ava
item.content:encoded:
Lee Berton, Wall Street Journal
June 1995

The Beatles meditated with an Indian guru. Shirley MacLaine touts reincarnation. Now singer Gino Vannelli says a Hindu monk’s advise is reshaping his life. The monk’s message of enlightenment: Get an accountant.

Mr. Vannelli, 42 years old, had a hit record called “I Just Wanna Stop” that sold a million copies in 1978 and made him a millionaire. But then things went downhill. He began spending $25,000 a month on new cars, supporting friends and relatives and buying new homes, he says. And because he didn’t have another his record, his outstanding bills rose to $250,000 or more, he adds.

Mr. Vannelli says he soon wanted to find “my God-essence and get my life back together.” So he became what he calls a Zen theosophist. He says he talked to Benedictine monks in Big Sur, Calif., Inca priests in Peru and Zen priest in Japan. “I began looking for a new direction,” he says. His manager, John Baruck, says Mr. Vannelli’s tastes in reading and thinking “went off the beaten track, looking for answers.” Mr. Baruck, who reads Robert Ludlum and Tom Clancy, says Mr. Vannelli began reading philosophy, poetry and “the wisdom of the ages.”

Then, Mr. Vannelli met a Hindu monk near Malibu, Calif. “We spoke about my psyche, how there is no body without spirituality and how people build their sand castles in the sky,” he says. “I had always thought that the philosopher’s stone was buried in the muck.”

Mr. Vannelli said that the monk closed his eyes, opened them and gazed far into the sky. “He emerged almost as if from a trance and then he faced me and said, ‘What you really need is a good accountant.'” Mr. Vannelli hired on in Portland, Ore., where he lives. The accountant told him to tone down his lifestyle, he says, noting, “I now drive a Honda Accord, live in a modest home and don’t go on fancy vacations.” He has paid off his and even saved enough to make a new album “Yonder Tree”, which hit the record stores last month.

Does Mr. Vannelli still meditate with monks and priests? He says not, explaining: “I’m too busy preparing for my next performances in Montreal and Japan.”

item.title: From Sex God To Truth Seeker
item.dc:creator: ava
item.content:encoded:
Nicholas Jennings, Maclean’s
June 5th, 1995

In the 1970’s, Montreal-born Gino Vannelli was the quintessential Italian stallion, a hairy-chested prince of synthesizer rock and disco pop. He was a genuine sex symbol, drawing thousands of screaming female fans to sold-out concerts across North America. But by the mid-1980’s, Vannelli had grown disillusioned with his macho image – and his Roman Catholic faith. Adopting an existentialist outlook, he went through a life-altering experience while hiking alone in the Peruvian Andes, coming face-to-face, he says, with a “superior being.”

That spiritual awakening has since led to an exhaustive study of Hindu, Buddhist and mystic Christian values. Four years ago, Vannelli left his longtime home in Los Angeles, moving with his wife and son to the quieter city of Portland, Ore. The following year, while on tour in Japan, he spent several weeks with Zen monks near Tokyo. Now, the 42-year-old Vannelli is surprising his followers again: his new recording, “Yonder Tree”, is a jazz-drenched – and soul-baring – account of his spiritual journey.

Recorded with an acoustic trio (pianist Randy Porter, bassist Phil Baker and drummer Graham Lear) and various guests, including the illustrious saxophonist Tom Scott, the album ventures musically into the lush, 1950s style reminiscent of Frank Sinatra’s romantic ballads. But Vannelli takes a decidedly un-jazzlike approach to his lyrics. Songs such as “A Little Bit Of Judas” and “Jehovah And All That Jazz” wrestle with issues of temptation and desire. “Fallen In Love”, which features a tap dance solo from Gregory Hines, charts Vannelli’s inner quest with such wry lines as, “Found Jesus and Sidhartha in a bar in Djakarta.” That decidedly personal lyrical agenda sets “Yonder Tree” apart from the work of Harry Connick Jr., Canada’s Holly Cole and other vocalists who have explored older jazz styles. But one sign that the jazz community is willing to give Vannelli serious consideration is his June 29 appearance at this summer’s Montreal International Jazz Festival.

Sitting in a Toronto cafe’ recently, Vannelli appeared unconcerned about his new album’s chances of commercial success. Wearing blue jeans, a black tuxedo jacket and tinted aviator shades, and without his Afro hairdo of the ’70s, the singer talked about how he came to make “Yonder Tree”. “I’ve always liked some of the jazz-standard melodies, the brush-sweeping ballads,” he said. “And I wanted to write something in that vein without sounding nostalgic.” He added: “The album represents the journey I’ve been on, and this wanting to break through and do something I’ve always wanted, without being afraid of whether or not I’m going to sell a lot of records.”

Vannelli notes that his father, Joseph, a onetime singer himself who died four months ago, was a big influence on the new album. “My father was a Sinatra aficionado who played me all those classic Sinatra albums from the late 50’s and early 60’s,” says Vannelli. “When you’re brought up with the best tunes and arrangements, it’s hard to top that. Sinatra’s singing was impeccable – everything a singer wants to be.”

One of three boys born to barber Joseph and his wife, Delia, Gino had his own rock band, the Cobras, before he reached his teens. After he and brother Joe formed another group, inspired by Motown and called the Jacksonville Five, Gino went solo and began shopping tapes of his music around. Traveling to Los Angeles in 1973, Gino landed a recording deal with A&M; Records, after impressing part-owner Herb Alpert with his vocals and charisma.

The singer’s albums over the next years spawned several hits, including “People Gotta Move” (1974) and “I Just Wanna Stop” (1978). Vannelli was soon touring the United States, opening for acts such as Stevie Wonder and Gladys Knight and the Pips. He earned several Grammy Nominations and, by the end of the 1970s, the Vannelli brothers — Gino, Joe and Ross — had established themselves as a powerful triumvirate, earning Juno Awards as Canada’s top male vocalist, producer and engineer respectively. Although Gino enjoyed one other major hit, 1985’s platinum-selling “Black Cars”, musical taste had largely overtaken him, and he became haunted by his image as a 25-year-old, self-described “stud.” In fact, the singer now says that the whole time he was idolized as a sex symbol he was deeply conflicted. “I was taught that my lusts and sex were something devilish,” says Vannelli, who attended a strict Roman Catholic school in Montreal and later became an alter boy. “The image that I portrayed and my feelings towards women were constantly on trial, and I wound up unhappy and confused.”

Having rediscovered a new, deeper faith, Vannelli seems more at peace with himself. On the liner notes to “Yonder Tree”, he thanks his wife, Patricia, and their eight-year-old son, Anton, for “putting up with this daylong dreamer, having to be pointed in the general direction of the corner grocery store.” But he dedicates the album to his late father who, he says, quit music out of fear of failure. Recalls Vannelli: “He once told me, ‘Don’t ever be like me.’ But we all feel that fear. I have to ask myself, ‘Will the public accept me, or can I grow old with them thinking that I’m not good anymore?’ That’s the trap of having been some sort of sex god. And it’s very hard to get past that.” During his spiritual wanderings of the past several years, Gino Vannelli has struggled to reinvent himself. On the evidence of “Yonder Tree”, he has at least succeeded in leaving the carnal side of his performance far behind.

item.title: Vannelli Gives Nod To Jazz In New Album
item.dc:creator: ava
item.content:encoded:
Paul Delean, The Gazette, Montreal
May 20th, 1995

Delia Vannelli got a belated Mother’s Day gift this week. It was a copy, hand-delivered by the man himself, of son Gino’s new jazz album, Yonder Tree. That’s right. Jazz album.

After 20 years in the rock-and-pop genre, the 43-year-old Montreal native decided to follow a new path. “I’m not a traditional jazz writer or singer,” he noted during a brief visit to the city. (He’ll return next month to perform at the Montreal International Jazz Festival.) “I’ve simply taken a sound from the ’30s, ’40s and ’50s, pop production and vocalization from my era, musicianship that is fusion, also from our era, lyrics from I don’t know what era that have an element of antagonism and inner conflict, topics of the day, and strung them together to make the album what it is.”

“What I was after above all was a simple sense of beauty. If I didn’t achieve that, I achieved nothing at all. Beauty has to be it’s most definitive and lasting point. If I didn’t make that, it doesn’t have much of a point.” Reaction has been strong, and mixed. Some people on the pop side consider it too bold a departure; some in the jazz field say it’s not pure jazz. “I’m glad I wasn’t aware of this (debate) while I was recording it,” Vannelli said. Lyrically, Yonder Tree is very much in the Vannelli tradition of intense social, spiritual and emotional probing and evaluation, what he calls his “internal dialogue.”

The songs come complete with references to Walter Whitman, Marx, Moliere, Blavatsky, Jesus, Siddhartha, Solomon, Judas, Gideon, Jehovah, Gabriel and Coltrane. It’s a long way from People Gotta Move. “I’ve got a lot of complex feelings about existence itself,” he said. “I’m a real devotee of the mystics. I understand them, have had much similar experiences.” But he says the album also has a lighter side, “unspoken humor that belies all the serious questioning,” and points as an example to the song A Little Bit Of Judas, which begins with the words “well, you can wear those pajamas/Like those Tibetan lamas all day.”

Personally, the singer of hits like I Just Wanna Stop, Living Inside Myself and Black Cars says he’s happier than he’s ever been. “I used to be too tied to my career. It’s a subsidiary of me. How I feel in my life, the people around me, am I happy where I’m at – those things are more important to me now.” Still, he’s thinking of relocating again, after moving from California to Portland, Ore., three and a half years ago with his wife and son.

“My son’s in the second grade and I’d like him to finish fourth grade in Portland, but I’m not sure I want to stay there (beyond that). Maybe we’ll let the wind carry our seeds somewhere else.” There is no tour yet built around Yonder Tree, only next month’s visit to the Montreal Jazz Festival.

“This is something I wanted to do especially for Montreal – play for people I know, sort of a homecoming, with only piano, vibes and bass. The farthest people will be 50 feet from me. We might even have a few people from the audience sit in for a few numbers; we definitely will have some guests from the festival sit in.”

Twenty years after becoming an international star, Vannelli said he still gets nervous coming home to play. “Some of the people have such expectations, a wide variety of expectations. It’s kind of like singing for my father (Russ, who died four months ago of cancer). There’s a sort of unspoken rivalry. You want to do good; you hope you don’t disappoint.”

item.title: A Letter by Gino
item.dc:creator: ava
item.content:encoded:
This letter can be found in the inner sleeve of the “Live In Montreal” CD.

My young son sleeps soundly tonight. His lids have fallen and shut like locked doors to a fortress high on a hill. His breath deep and easy, his little body limp and sprawled tell me all is well on his mountaintop. Princess rescued and hero intact; enviable. I don’t know perhaps it is a question of untamed passions or unbridled desires but a courious incompatibility still remains between the night and sleep for me. It is as if only when the city sleeps I can hear the truest texture of the inner voice. I am in complete possession of my breath and heartbeat. It is as it always was, a kind of birthing process that first begins in the dark and silent womb of a solitary place. Where every thought, every motion, and every sound matters. Where the small becomes great and the great explodes and vanishes into the black of space and is born small again. Where the first and last battle is fought, legions of both higher and fallen angels merge and contract to a pinpoint and then blaze like the light of a thousand suns. It is the ritual of the deepest dreaming. It is the courting of the muse. A sense of grace and fortune overcome me. I am at ease. I neither bear the searing wounds of failure nor the weight and disorientation of overwhelming commercial success. I feel as Fredrick Prokosh, the novelist once wrote of his life and career; too much acceptance would have spoiled him, too little would have embittered his heart.

I am alluding to a certain kind of freedom, creative freedom, one of the rarest of all gifts that has only to be believed in and pursued in earnest to receive. From the day my brother Joe and I stormed the gates of A&M; Records and were embraced by Herb Alpert and Jerry Moss, it has been too easy to take for granted and artist’s inborn right of expression. I say this because once I was robbed of it. Only then did I realize the preciousness of my lost possession.

The boombox plays in the background. I listen to Enzo, Mike, Maxayne and brother Joe offering themselves to the music. I gaze down, shake my head and smile at the sound of familiar words and melodies that come from my own voice. I think back to those endless days of desire and determination, the idols of my past, the need to be like them, the dream to an accepted artist, whatever the cost. It is a time when the blindness of youth is a blessing, when the failings of inexperience are forgiven and compensated by the natural wisdom of instinct and willpower. It is strange, the songs not only kill me quietly with memories but inspire me to go forward in any direction undaunted by new impediments. Maybe I am falling in love with life all over again. Suddenly I don’t mind dog days and sleepless nights as much. I extend my hands outward in thanks to those who are listening and remembering after my twelve year absence from the stage. I turn upward and inward for still deeper thanks.

Can’t help staring at my boy, can’t help wondering what he’ll think of “I Just Wanna Stop” or “Living Inside Myself” in twenty or thirty years from now. I wonder how these times will fare in his eyes when he’s a man. the tape machine has switched off, no more thoughts. I will lay at his feet, close my eyes and join him in his hilltop.

Gino

item.title: Vannelli Returning To The Stage At A Critical Career Point
item.dc:creator: ava
item.content:encoded:
Evelyn Erskine, The Ottawa Citizen
November 16, 1990

Twelve years ago, Gino Vannelli moved to Los Angeles,the home of the music business. Montreal’s man with the big voice became visible to the industry, but disappeared from his fans. The move worked. His albums, laden with the synthesized dance hits of the day such as Black Cars and People Gotta Move, were usually successful despite his hiatus from performing. But now, Vannelli has reached a critical point in his life, which is starkly chronicled in his current release Inconsolable Man. He is turning the tables around. The singer-songwriter is now looking, for a ranch in rural Oregon where he plans to raise his four-year-old son. And after much soul-searching, he has jumped back into the spotlight for his first tour since 1978, including a date at the Congress Centre Monday.

Vannelli is uncertain how the process began, saying it was never part of any grand plan. “I got burned out in the early days,” he said. “I went through personal changes where I wasn’t sure whether I wanted to go out on the road anymore. Then I got the itch. I came to the point where I knew I wouldn’t be happy if I didn’t get back out there.” It has taken Vannelli more than six months to prepare for his return to the road, both psychologically and physically, “I realized that if I were to go back out I would have to be strong. I started hiking on long trails, doing martial arts two or three times a week. I got to the point where I was running four miles a day. “But all of that is blown out the window when you hit the stage. That hour and a half is so intense. It has a life and timing of its own.”

Vannelli has never been known as a soul-baring singer-songwriter. There was always an elusive buffer between the man and the music. Inconsolable Man is different: it is a personal album and those personal feelings are made public. “Sometimes you feel your chest is out there with a bull’s-eye sign and people are just throwing darts at it”.But Vannelli never allowed himself to think about public perception when he wrote the songs. “Heavens no. If I did that I would never write.” For Vannelli, Inconsolable Man was an essential journey. It put him in touch with diverse religions and philosophies including Zen Buddhism, Hinduism and mystical Christianity.

“When you are inconsolable, you look for answers. Some would go back to the roots. For me, I started reading the esoteric arts. I wanted to know why I felt what I felt,” he said. “And I began to understand wonderful philosophies and ways of life that people all over this planet are practising and believing. For me, it was the only way out of an otherwise vicious cycle that keeps spiralling and spiralling until you die.”

Much of this turnaround can be attributed to the birth of Vannelli,’s first child four years ago. He started to take a harder look at the world he had brought his son into. Sometimes feelings of futility take over as in Rhythm Of Romance. “There is this realization that I can do nothing about it. I can only talk about it, laugh at it, poke at it, then turn away from it for awhile.” Several songs are graphic portrayals of the street life in Los Angeles. Vannelli looked at his own young son and decided he would move to to rural Oregon where his wife hails from.

Yet Vannelli understands that he has a choice while most other parents in L.A. probably do not, so he selects his words carefully. “I don’t want to sit here and say by moving my son out, that I am condemning millions of children living there. This is personal preference. I would prefer that he be brought up in a rural atmosphere and go to the city when he wants to go to the city.” There is no reason to believe that Vannelli’s next album will be much like Inconsolable Man. Then, he will likely be in a new, more relaxed setting and will have relived the excitement of the road.

Inconsolable Man reflects an important point in Vannelli’s life which he feels everyone experiences at some stage. He is not concerned that his audience may not accept his introspective side. “If I viewed my audience as just people who bought Black Cars, I may not have recorded an album like this. But I don’t. I view them as having the same thoughts and having the same questions. I am totally at ease in knowing they have a sympathetic vibration to it. I don’t think they see the darkness as much as the longing to get out of it.”
item.excerpt:encoded: an article with Gino Vannelli from the November 1990 edition of The Ottawa Citizen

item.title: Performance, Not Promotion, Drives Vannelli Back To The Stage
item.dc:creator: ava
item.content:encoded:
Kim Hughes, Now-Toronto
November 8th, 1990

It’s hard to say if Gino Vannelli’s first tour in 12 years is doing much to reinforce a more contemporary sound and image for the singer, or if that’s his intention. While the 84 release of the single Black Cars, accompanied by a slick video with androgynous looking models, showed Vannelli’s willingness to break new ground. old, notions die hard. Vannelli remains strongly associated with the 70s disco era and its trappings the gold chains, wide-open shirts and tight trousers.

All it takes is a phone call to the Diamond – where Vannelli gives two shows next week – to learn that his sex-symbol image still holds.Says Diamond promotions person Dawna Vinnels. calls about ticket information and seating arrangements have been pouring in. most from middle-aged women. “When I tell them they can get as close to him as his knees,” Vinnels says, “I can practically hear them swoon. For his part, Vannelli jokingly rejects the idea that he’s a “lady killer.””I never killed one lady in my life,” he says. But the point is taken. So why tour now? “This is for myself.” Vannelli says. “I don’t care what the turnout is, what people’s preconceptions are. I just needed to go out. Doing this reflects a much deeper, deeper decision than just going out on the road because my album needs promoting or my image needs boosting.

“I love singing and I haven’t done that in front of people for 12 years. I began feeling like a pent up animal, a tiger in a cage. and when I get on that stage. I start to blow it all out. “When Black Cars came out. it felt like a new beginning,” the soft spoken singer continues. “But I wasn’t sure if I was really ready. I could have toured, there would have been an audience, but I think I was going through some personal growth thing. I didn’t want to be half there. I didn’t want to be a potpourri of a person.” Indeed, the last few years have witnessed significant changes in Vannelli’s career and personal life as well as his image. A switch from longtime label A & M to PolyGram, and the birth of his first child have both figured in. And he’s continued to sell records – by the million.

So is this jaunt with a full band away of paying back fans who’ve re-mained faithful throughout his career? “I’m not sure that I felt I owed them anything,” he says. “When you put it like that, maybe I do owe them something. I never thought about it. “You have to understand something,” he explains. “The 70’s was a whole different era. A lot of artists performing today, if they had been around in the 70s, they ‘would have been really pooh-poohed. “Picture Prince or someone like that performing in the days when the Eagles were really hot. The mind set was post-Woodstock. So I think I was mismatched to an era.
item.excerpt:encoded: an article with Gino Vannelli from the November 8th, 1990 edition of NOW-Toronto

item.title: Vannelli’s A New Man
item.dc:creator: ava
item.content:encoded:
Neal Watson, The Edmonton Sun
November 2nd, 1990

The image has never done him justice.To this day when Gino Vannelli’s name is mentioned, it conjures up images of the darkest days of pop music in the 70s. Vannelli, shirt open to expose his hairy chest, is crooning one of his two huge hits of the ’70s, People Gotta Move and I Just Want to Stop..But, in Vannelli’s defence, certain things should be pointed out. The Montreal native survived disco and continues his successful recording career, the latest chapter of which is his new album, Inconsolable Man. Vannelli’s huge hit singles, 1985’s Black Cars and 87’s Wild Horses, were two of his strongest songs. How many other artists even remotely associated with the disco era have prospered into the 90s?

Today, 38-year-old Gino Vannelli, the married father of a four-year-old son, is centuries removed from that past. On his first major, tour in 11 years, he performs in Edmonton next Tuesday at the Dinwoodie Lounge at the University of Alberta.Soft-spoken and thoughtful. the title of his new album, Inconsolable Man, says a lot about the searching he did while writing songs for this record.Vannelli, interviewed from his Los Angeles home,speaks of his “cathartic or spiritual awakening.”You realize the things you do as an artist can be destructive to the other person in the house”he says.Artists like to live in a destructive way. It fuels the fire”. Becoming a father prompted Vannelli to reconsider the way he lived his life. But it’s been a long, slow process “You find things to light your fire that are not destructive,” he says. “It’s a whole behavioral change. You can’t just live for the music”.

Between the ages of 20 and 27, Vannelli toured 200 nights a year. It burned him out. Although he admits to being anxious about performing in front of audiences again, Vannelli is confident he’s found the right formula to “integrate technology with the human players.”The last big change (for the time being) that Vannelli plans to make is a move from his home for the past 12 years, Los Angeles.Crime, congestion and the craziness of life in southern California have convinced Vannelli that’s it’s not the place where he wants to bring up his child. He is thinking of moving either to the Pacific Northwest in the U.S. or Vancouver. “I’m still going through a changing time. I’m feeling pretty good about it.”
item.excerpt:encoded: an interview with Gino Vannelli from the November 2nd, 1990 edition of The Edmonton Sun

item.title: Gino & Joe Vannelli – A Family Affair
item.dc:creator: ava
item.content:encoded:
By Oliver Cauvin
Keyboards #37, October 1990

Since 1973, Gino Vannelli have recorded 10 major albums, some of them produced with the help of Ross, their other brother. Being at ease in jazz, jazz rock, symphonic and now, FM rock. Their sound and moods are instantly recognizable, due mostly to their use of synths.

As a preview to their first European tour, and in France in November and December 1990, they reveal themselves to Keyboards.

You were among the first to use synths in song writing and arranging. What made you go in that direction?

Joe: As a piano player, keyboards always interested me. It was Gino’s idea to use synths. We had very little to work with in 1973 and we did our best with what we had. But when I see what’s around today, it’s incredible! Keyboards are becoming more and more important now.

Is the exclusive use of synths a good thing in your opinion?

Joe: It depends on how it’s done, the people behind it all and the way they use this new instrument.

I agree completely! In the past few albums, ‘Black Cars’ for example, you get the impression that you’ve only used Yamahas. Was that the case?

Joe: You’re not the first one to say that, but they’re not the main instruments, if you can believe it. We mostly used Memorymoogs on ‘Black Cars’.

MIDIfied?

Joe: I don’t remember using that much MIDI 1984. In fact, almost everything was recorded live on that album. Sequencers weren’t as sophisticated as they are now, and I only used a QX1 to get the the songs ready, and it was a pain to program!

The only MIDI instrument we used on ‘Black Cars’ was a DX7 and the only sequencer was a Roland (which I don’t remember the specs), for a drum roll. We use them more often now.

What decided you to use the new technology, when you had such a warm sound with Prophets or Oberheims?

Joe: It’s true we used Oberheims then, but we were looking for new sounds. When we heard the digital sounds, we were amazed by their clearness and definition. Analog sounds are great, but they all sound the same.

And you don’t get that impression with digital sounds?

Joe: It all depends on the arranging. We’ve tried using both recently. In general, we use analog synths for what we call texture pads for warmer sounds, and digital synths for bell-type sounds or sounds that need a certain edge.

Why did you sample Jimmy Haslip’s bass instead of having him play on ‘Inconsolable Man’?

Joe: (laughs) Jimmy was so busy that he only had a few days for us. Since he has such a nice sound, I asked him if I could sample some.

These samples were combined with synths so they wouldn’t look too artificial. Samples often sound horrible because the same note is triggered different ways. It lacks expression.

You’ve tried for a long time to mix synths with acoustic instruments. The violins on ‘Pauper In Paradise’ for example come to mind. Who came up with the idea?

Joe: The B side on that album is essentially made of real strings. My brother had written that piece a long time before. We’d just made two albums with a lot of synths and we thought it would be a different way of working. We left for London and hooked up with Don Sebesky for the orchestration. I remember Gino playing the themes on piano and Don writing the notes as we were going along. We didn’t even record him a demo!

We started by recording the synths for the A side, then the third movement for the B side and overdubbed the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra. We’ll play a song from that album on this tour and we’ll use computers to program the strings with the Kurzweill. I think people will be surprised by how real it will sound. We’ve been working on this tour for over a month and there will be a lot of MIDI.

Will you sample the sounds directly from the master tapes?

Joe: No. I already have the sounds, since I’ve made them. We’ll use the computers for all program changes and to help us between songs.

Can you define your roles in producing, songwriting and arranging?
