Joe: Gino is better placed to answer that question.

Gino: It’s hard to explain a process that looks like chemistry, but I’ll try! Let’s take for example ‘Moment To Moment’ or ‘If I Should Lose This Love’. In essence, I write the songs, and we try to see in studio what they’re all about. We work hand in hand, go forward, then back, try new ideas and erase them. If I choose not to work on an idea, Joe will pick it up and rework it. For ‘Shame’, I only had a few parts and Joe had a song he couldn’t finish. We just put them together. Sometimes, it’s made of bits and pieces.

For ‘Rhythm Of Romance’, the author went in studio hoping I’d tell him what I thought of it, and in fact, I didn’t like it very much. I sat down on the piano, suggested some improvement, and we had a brand new piece!

Joe: Producing-wise, if the keyboard part has rhythm to it, we’ll put together a roll, bass drum and piano to see how it sounds. But generally speaking, with never begin a song with a definite bar pattern; it the melody that counts.

You’ve just talked about ‘Shame’. there is a great voice in there, a very low voice that sounds like a ‘varyspeed’.

Joe: Not at all. It’s Kevin Dorsey’s voice, and it hasn’t been worked on.

I see that Mark Craney is playing again with you. His health must have improved.

Gino: Yes. He played on ‘The Time Of Day’ and a couple of other songs on the album. He also worked on the first album of a Scandinavian band we produced.

Joe: He really made a miraculous recovery!

Gino: For that piece we recorded a year ago, Mark came to the studio on a wheelchair and with his crutches. He could barely move, but sat behind drum pads linked to a computer. He almost couldn’t hold a stick with his right hand, but his left hand was OK. We overdubbed a lot, his ideas were good as usual and he gained confidence. Now he’s playing real drums five nights a week in clubs. I don’t think he’ll tour with us because it’s very tiring, but maybe in a year or two. He called me the other day after he learned that we were auditioning drummers for the tour and he was a little upset that we didn’t call him!

How do you record the synths? Mono, stereo, with lots of effects? There is such a wide variety of sounds!

Gino: Since we have a very “ochestral” and wide sound, we have to record in stereo, which enhances the textures.

Joe: We also add digital effects, echoes, delays reverbs and “spacial expanders”.

Jimmy Haslip has told me of an album on which he played that was never released. What about it? Will you ever release it?

Gino: It’s here on a shelf somewhere (laughs). This is an unavoidable thing in an artist’s career. I don’t think I’ll release it, even if it were remixed. However, it’s quite probable that I might use some of the songe. It was done around 1982-1983, but our recording techniques have changed so much since then that it wouldn’t hold its own.

Both of you do some programming. Do you start from scratch or do you change already existing sounds?

Gino: It depends. We sometimes make our own samples. For example, if we like the sound pf a snare drum for a song, we might change its tons or add something to make it clearer. We never keep a rough sound.

On “Shame”, the snare comes from a lower end Yamaha BAR to which we added a digital sample to make it sound bigger. We also added some real snare drum vibrations. This way, we can keep the medium notes and have a fatter sound on the highs.

Gino, you’ve launched the career of many great musicians over the years: Jay Graydon in 1975, Carlos Rios in 1978, Mike Miller and Vinnie Colaiuta in 1981. Do you get the impression that you are some kind of a talent scout?

Gino: (Laughs) Maybe we are. It’s true that a lot of people seem to have gained notoriety after playing on our albums, and I’m really happy for them. Too bad for me they ask for a better pay!!! We stay real close though. When I asked Mike Miller to go on tour with us, he accepted right away and cancelled all his other gigs. When Maxayne Lewis, our backup singer works with other people, she asks for a certain rate, and for at least three hours. But when she’s with us, she stays 3-4 hours and tells me: “Pay me what you want”. It must come from the way we work with our musicians.

What’s happening with your brother Ross? Why isn’t he on this album? It looks as if he’s very much in demand as a songwriter isn’t he?

Gino: We realized we didn’t need to be three. Also Ross has his own studio and production company. Joe and I spend so much time in studio trying new stuff that we may be too slow for Ross.

Will you keep producing other acts?

Gino: Absolutely. The first new act was the Scandinavian band I mentionned earlier. I think people will like their music. It’s progressive pop sung by two guys, pretty much in the spirit of Tears For Fears, and produced by our people. Medley Records, a label from over there, is helping them.

You’ve made a major change in your songwriting, by going more towards a pop and FM sound Aren’t you afraid to lose your old fans? Is this a personal decision or something coming from the record company?

Gino: It’s really a personal choice. It’s a lot of fun! But I think the next album will be very different. I don’t think my fans will be bothered by the new songs, but who’s to say? I’ll find out at the end of the tour; if people boo me, I’ll know what I’ll have to do. However, I think my pop songs are very different from what you can hear on radio today.

Can you tell us about the equipment you use in studio?

Joe: Let’s see… It’s very conventional: DX7, D50, Kawai, Kurzweill, Prophet, Moog, Akai samplers. We have Lexicon 480, Yamaha, and Alesis. Alesis especially is excellent!

Do you record everything in digital or do you still use analog?

Joe: On the last album, the ‘orchestration’ was done live by computer, but we used an analog ‘console’ for the vocals and guitar. We mixed in ½ inch analog using Dolby SR. I also used DAT, but I prefer the sound of the half inch with Dolby SR. It adds a lot of musicality, and you get rid of the extremes. When you use a lot of digital, the sound becomes very rough; analog smoothens it up. A lot of people do that, like Bruce Swedien who records for Quincy Jones and Michael Jackson. He records all drum parts on analog, then transfers them on digital to get a little compressionand a slightly lower sound. I think the best way to record is by using a potpourri of different techniques, where you record some instruments on digital and others on digital.

Gino, I often heard people say that you are a frustrated opera singer! How do you respond to that?

Gino: (Laughs) I don’t know! First, I don’t feel frustrated at all, but I think I understand what they mean…

Will you go back to acoustic instruments in the future?

Gino: I believe so, simply due to the fact that if you love music, you get tired of always doing the same thing. Going from one thing to another brings more pleasure out of your own work. I don’t know yet where I’ll go. For the moment, we concentrate on getting ready for this tour. This is the first time we’ll play in Europe.

Translated from French by Claude Champagne
item.excerpt:encoded: An interview with Joe and Gino Vannelli as featured in Keyboards Magazine October 1990

item.title: The Comeback Of Gino Vannelli
item.dc:creator: ava
item.content:encoded:
Gavin Report
September 1985

Gino Vannelli has spent more than half his life making music. Along with brothers Joe and Ross, Gino was influenced by early R&B; legends James Brown and Otis Redding.By the mid-seventies he was signed to A&M; Records and he became an early proponent al synthesizers. After a string of choice singles and intriguing albums, his career came to a sudden halt in 1981.He still can’t quite explain away his absence, but the recent success of his comeback single, “Black Cars” and the recent release of his latest single, “Hurts To Be In Love,” make up for lost time. Gino is also about ready to take up live performance again and may make his re debut at the upcoming Canadian Live-Aid concert.

RF: I was surprised to learn your roots were actually in Canada. Where did you grow up?
GV: Montreal, Canada. Montreal was not much of a city then. I grew up quickly in the 60’s.

RF: You certainly have a grasp for production, at least you know how to get yourself to do what you need to do. As teenagers, you and your brothers put together a band called the Jacksonville Five.
GV: Umm-humm.

RF: Were you having fun with another band with a similar name?
GV: We put that together in 1965. I think the Jackson Five was in ’69.

RF: So we could clear that up that you were not trying to have fun with the Jackson Five at that point.
GV: No no. R&B; was getting very big in Montreal, and we were a bit of a bar band. We really wanted to emulate our black heroes.

RF: Who were those heroes?
GV: Oh yeah, all those records that were sort of a beginning underground records that became universal records: James Brown, Otis Redding, The Bar-Kays, The Chiffons, The Orions, The Teflons.

RF: (Laughter)
GV: And at that time Patti LaBelle too. All the Apollo. I can’t even remember a lot of them now, but we were just tremendous fans of those records then. So we said The Jacksonville Five was a hip black band and we were just white, lower middle class, rural Italian boys.

RF: (Laughs) Doing R&B?
GV: Yeah.

RF: We know that you do almost all your work with your two brothers. Where do you fit chronologically with brothers Joe and Ross?
GV: Joe is the oldest. I’m the middle, and Ross the youngest. We have been working together for a long time. I guess maybe it was out of convenience at first and then we sort of realized we depended on each other’s talents.

RF: Still as a teenager you signed with RCA for Canada and had a minor experience of some type there. Apparently that music didn’t cross over the border. But how did you end up making contact with A&M; Records?
GV: It actually started from the day I signed with RCA in Montreal. That further lead me exploring avenues in New York and then I followed avenues that I explored and failed in New York. I moved on to LA. So I guess it’s the domino theory. Getting to A&M; was at first no easy task then all of a sudden it just fell like matter from the sky out of nowhere.

RF: Were you and your brother showcasing in L.A. and someone discovered you?
GV: No, nothing like that. A lot more, again it was sort of a low-class dream. You’re there and you’re hoping to meet somebody. You’re hoping somebody is going to walk by or be at the right place at the right time. All the drama and then you swear you hear timpani in your head. We were there for three or four months, trying to meet people. Finally, our money ran out and I decided I was going to try to barge through the gates of A&M; and try to meet Herb Alpert or wait until he came out of his office and just run up to him and see what happened. I found the locked up gates and I said it was now or never because I had a flight out in two days after that. I just barged through the gates and put out my hand and hoped he wouldn’t punch me out or sick the guard on me. But he started talking to me and was very gracious. He allowed me to play some songs for him and became very interested. Two days later I was signed to A&M; Records.

RF: And how long did that relationship last professionally?
GV: Oh, it lasted from ’73-74 to 1979. So,it was a good five or six years there.

RF: And probably two of your biggest hits came during that era.”People Gotta Move” and “I Just Wanna Stop.” How did those records affect you? Did everything seem to accelerate with having successful records?
GV: Well, I never looked at it, unfortunately perhaps, much to my chagrin. I never really looked at music as a means of getting monetary satisfaction. It was all very serious to me. I did what I a to do to feel self-satisfied … proving myself that I was an artist that I was worthy of whatever it is that makes an artist think he is an artist. To me, each album was just another chapter.

RF: You did seem to go from a singles philosophy into more thematic thing. You were stretched out. The songs seemed to be getting longer as the albums went along.
GV: Yeah, and I think it was also a sign of the times. Music was a little more experimental in the 70’s, it wasn’t as formulized as today. Artists were trying things. So we experimented very much with synthesizers and extra parts of songs and working on songs of “theme” rather than three minute songs.

RF: What are your thoughts now with pop music being dominated so much by synthesizers? Do you think we could be guilty of some overkill? Or do you like the flexibility the synthesizer type machines afford the artist?
GV: I think you have answered some of the question, but I look at instruments as vocabulary. I look at instruments as the means. But it is not the end, by far. You can be modern. You can be a modern thinking man. You can be a man who is contemporary and perhaps further the contemporary senses milling around in your mind and not even get close to a synthesizer and be just as modern and just as progressive as anybody else. I think people who depend on synthesizers to bring across modern thought and modern wave lengths are probably going to be the first to be accused of overkill. But the people who use a synthesizer as an instrument, as they would a violin, or a guitar, I don’t think they are ever going to hurt their careers or their music. You can’t say to yourself,”We’re going to be an all synthesizer band,” because you might as well call yourself The Synthesizers. First you’ve got to make good music, then use whatever you have available to further along that goal.

RF: You seem to be saying that you’ve got to be “saying” something on top of that music.
GV: Obviously everybody has access to the same synthesizers. Everybody has access to the props and programmers are the same. But it’s going to go in waves … perhaps in the future in some minor rebellion against synthesizers, but obviously we’re becoming more digitized and more electronically inclined. But that should just help us get our point across that much more pleasantly.

RF: You’ve been missing for most of the last four or five years. What was your last record before Black Cars?
GV: Nightwalker in ’81.

RF: Where have you been the last four years?
GV: Well, I don’t think I can answer that take place before I could be as honest as I would like to be. All I could say is I really couldn’t come out with the whole truth without being a little too candid. So I’d rather just say some things happened in my career that were unforeseen. I had a noose around my neck. I think I finally got that off.

RF: At least you’re back on the airwaves and you’ve got product in the stores. Actually, part of your re-birth took place in Europe. The album we now have on our desks was out in Europe last Fall. Was there something from a contractual standpoint that made it easier to release product in Europe?
GV: It was all part of the knots of the noose around my neck. It was very difficult to make any kind of move upwards, downwards, or laterally in the United States. So I had to just go where it was less conspicuous. And things started happening for me first in France and then PolyGram picked up world wide. Then it got over to the states and finally people started thinking I was marketable enough and viable. Because, on top of being away for four or five years, a lot of things have changed in music, including the visual revolution. A lot of people had this sexist misconception on the interpretation of who they thought I was. It was very difficult after three, four, five years away to let people know who I really was.

RF: We talked about this noose around your neck. Did this prevent you from performing live? Or was it something you didn’t feel the need to perform? In other words, were you also out of the live arena during the same period of time?
GV: Yes, indirectly it does because honestly a sound-minded artist knows he’s not going to go on any kind of graveyard shift and you’re not going to start performing songs of the dead. I’m just too young to be playing golden oldies.

RF: Between the last Arista album and this one, you seemed to have gone through an image change as well. In coming back, were you looking for a specific image outside of your music?
GV: Yeah … But not really much. I think the whole world got a haircut since 1980, so I don’t think I’m really alone in that respect.

RF: How do you feel your music has changed during your lay-over?
GV: I don’t feel that objective about myself to comment on myself. All I can say is that as an artist I try my best to deal with all the obstacles … all the adversities that I’m dealing with and the first being the energy from within. When you’re dealing with the part of music that is the business part of it, in some way you have to maintain your artistry. I think you know what I’m really comfortable around you.

RF: Sure.
GV: You have to be very aware of the fact that you have record companies and agents and it really should be second nature. But many times, when you’re trying to get back into the race, back into the business you’re all so aware of it you’re “hyper” aware of it.

RF: The current album, in lyrical tone, is reasonably somber Could we assume there is a little bk of autobiographical material in the album?
GV: I think the groove you happen to be in at the time will usually be reflected in the songs you’re writing at the time. And I guess “Just A Motion Away” and “Total Stranger” and a few of the other tracks are very much reflective of an isolationist kind of a feeling.

RF: Black Cars, which proved to be a very successful re-introduction for you, also had an outrageous video and a lot of people may not have caught some of the things in the video. Did you play an active role in the concept of the video?
GV: Yeah, I think it was a pretty good video. Derek Burvick is a good director. Its not exactly how I felt at first but it grew on me.

RF: Do you feel it may have narrowed the listener’s interpretation of the song down?
GV: No, I don’t think it narrowed down. I think on the up-side it probably at least focused a little bit on what the song was really about. A lot of people have no idea what the song was about. The song was about people with things to hide.

RF: The current single, “Hurts To Be In Love,” which is off to a very fast start with pop radio, is an extreme departure from Black Cars, in that the tempo is much more moderate. It’s very much in a ballad style. But is this more you? Are you comfortable with this kind of song, or do you like to move it up and down?
GV: Well, even as we speak I’ve written 25 new songs for the next album. So, that album is already history for me and I’m on to something new. So I can’t really look at one song and say “this is me” or “that’s where I should be.” I’m just one of those thick-headed people who just wants to be or remain an artist I went through it all and I’m just going to write whatever is most compelling or is really bothering me at the time that I think should be put on paper.

RF: The Canadian Live Aid thing. Do you have any thoughts on that?
GV: Yeah, I’m petrified.

RF: In what respect?
GV: Well, it’s strange because in the 70’s I based my career basically on live performing. I guess I should be confident But it’s been so long since I’ve been on stage. It has been six or seven years. All I keep doing is practicing in my living room and doing whatever I can do to build up confidence. I don’t know, I’ve been toying with the fact that I might go and do a couple of songs as a guest or something like that.
item.excerpt:encoded: An interview with Gino Vannelli from the September 1985 edition of The Gavin Report

item.title: The Vannelli Brothers
item.dc:creator: ava
item.content:encoded:
Keyboards Magazine, 1979

The Vannelli Bros. One of them is the Star — the one with the golden voice, the dramatic stage persona, the matted chest hair, the Grammy nomination, the Hunk Of The Month award from Sixteen magazine. The other one is the Shadow — somewhat to the rear, on the edge of the spotlight, in the dim gleam of the LEDs behind his synthesizers. Only one of them gets his face and pectoral forestry splashed onto magazine covers, but when it comes to making music, especially with regard to using keyboards to their best effect, it takes both of the Vannelli brothers –Gino the Star and Joe the Shadow — to get the job done.

Working with a variety of other musicians, a third brother, Ross, often among them on guitar and vocals, the Vannellis have been laying down ambitious pop-rock tracks for years. Their style seems to lie just beyond the traditional limits of AM radio, in that Gino’s compositions and arrangements are frequently more distended, his productions deeper and more Spectorian, than the usual Top 40 fare. In a format regularly saturated with formula music, where string players are unseen and almost unheard behind disco drums, the Vannelli brothers have hired the entire Royal Philharmonic Orchestra and used it as a prominent element in varying musical textures, together with Joe’s electric keyboards and Gino’s piano playing [A Pauper In Paradise, A&M;, SP-4664).

In spite of this typically grandiose approach, the Vannellis continue to produce accessible albums, partly because Gino’s personality as a singer cuts like a beacon through even the most involved charts. At the heart of his performance lies a love of jazz and rock, implanted by his father, a hairdresser and former big-band leader with a liking for Miles Davis and John Coltrane, and by his childhood experiences in the local Montreal music scene. While older brother Joe was practicing piano, Gino was inspired by a film of Gene Krupa to begin playing drums on a second-hand set, and at the age of 12 he started playing high school gigs with a band called the Cobras. After a year, the brothers joined forces in the Jacksonville Five, a soul band patterned after the music of James Brown and the Stax Records artists.

Eventually the Vannellis saved enough money to invest in a four-track tape deck and equipment, and soon they were at work preparing a demo tape in their own basement studio to hustle in Los Angeles. Even in those early days, keyboards played a large role in their arrangements, although at first this was due mainly to financial constraints. As Gino recently told Canadian Musician magazine, they had tried to line up a guitarist to play on the tape, but each one they talked to wanted to be paid, “and frankly, we just couldn’t afford any extra expenses, so we started using the synthesizer instead. I guess it was the root of the evolution.”

Gino had briefly been contracted — at the age of 15, no less — to RCA, and had released a single the following year that made it into the Canadian Top 10, but from the beginning the Vannellis had their eyes set on the bigger markets south of the border. Two years spent in New York as a songwriter whetted Gino’s taste for the business even more, and as his performing and composing talents continued to mature, it seemed only a question of time before his efforts would be rewarded.

The jackpot was struck in 1973, when Gino and Joe cut their debut LP, Crazy Life [A&M;, 4395]. Powerful People [A&M;, 3630] followed, and then came the third album, Storm At Sunup [A&M;, 4533], in which Joe’s synthesizer work began to be brought further into the foreground. Their latest releases are Gist Of The Gemini [A&M;, 4596], A Pauper In Paradise, and the platinum-selling Brother To Brother [A&M;, 4722].

The critics as well as the fans have praised the Vannelli albums over the years. Recently nominated for a Grammy award in the Male Pop Vocal Performance category for “I Just Wanna Stop,” off the Brother To Brother LP, Gino has received a Juno award, the Canadian equivalent of a Grammy, in the same category, and two of his albums have won Grammys for Best Engineering.

Although he played drums on Crazy Life, Gino hasn’t done any drumming in the studio since then. When he does perform on an instrument nowadays, it is the piano, and when not actually at the keyboards, he is developing his ideas of how to use them with Joe. The attention that they devote to these instruments is evident in their recent LPs and concert tours, in which other keyboardists are often used. Richard Baker, for example, who would later work with Gary Wright [see CK, May ’78], plays several keyboards on Gist Of The Gemini, and synthesist Leon Gaer doubles bass lines with bass guitarist Jimmy Haslip on Brother To Brother.

Since the Vannelli keyboard sound is the product of both Gino’s and Joe’s creativity, CK spoke with the two of them individually in order to focus on their own respective approaches. The following interviews, like their two symbiotic personalities, together offer a subtle insight into the singular success of the Vannelli brothers.

Gino Vannelli

Was the piano playing of your big brother Joe one of the main things that led you into music?
No, actually; it was the opposite way around. Joe was in college and I was in my last year of high school when I started writing. After a year in college I planned to go on with my career in music, so I made my way down to New York when I was around 17. Joey used to come and help me now and then in sessions, but it wasn’t until maybe a year and a half to two years later that he followed me full time. I was mostly a drummer then.

Do you still consider the drums to be your primary instrument?
Well, it’s the instrument that I once knew the most about, I think. If you don’t practice or continually get into an instrument, though, it really falls to the wayside very quickly, and I stopped playing drums by 1972 or something like that, so it’s been a long time. I do intend to play some drums again, maybe on our next tour and on a cut or two from the next album, but it’s mainly keyboard that I play now.

How often do you play keyboards onstage?
Basically on just one or two songs. I think I did it on “Ugly Man” [from Gist Of The Gemini] most recently, and on the tour before the last one I played on “Black And Blue” [from A Pauper In Paradise].

Do you stick to the piano, or do you play other keyboards as well?
No, it’s just the piano. I usually play it during a solo song, where it’s just me playing and singing.

Do you have a particular favorite piano?
We really like the Bosendorfer at AIR Studios in London. This one’s a nine-foot model worth about forty grand; it’s really hard to say exactly. Something happened to it, though, and it has lost its tone. Too many people abused it, too many cokes were spilled on the keyboard. I like the Yamaha acoustic piano too. I mean, there’s no doubt that the Yamaha is a good piano — I have one myself — but I think there is really no match for some of the older Steinways from the ’40s or ’50s and some of their big nine-foot models. The earlier Steinways have that certain tone that’s really great.

What kind of action do you like on a piano?
I think a medium action is good for me. I don’t like it too high and too heavy, and I don’t like it too low and too light either. I like a medium action that’s maybe a little on the stiff side. I prefer a big-sounding piano to a muffled, very untrebly piano. I like a piano that’s bright and just kind of shines, rather than a piano with a thin sound. Some of the Bosendorfers can get real thin when you get above the C one octave up from Middle C.

How is the piano amplified onstage?
We only used one acoustic piano this time out, and we had Helpinstill pickups on it. it’s just too much of a hassle, though. The Helpinstill is the best of its sort, but it picks up a lot of ground loops and radio station buzzes. It’s just another mechanical toy that could go wrong.

How do you mike the piano in the studio?
There’s really no set rule. Some pianos are too bright to mike closely, and some are too dull to mike from a distance. It could involve putting mikes inside, it could be just opening the piano and setting the mikes only a few feet away, or it could be shoving the mikes right near the strings and hammers, closing the top, and putting a cover on it. Some pianos sound good when you mike them from underneath, some pianos sound good when you play them on a tile floor, and some pianos just sound terrible when they’re on tile. I mean, it really all depends on the piano. You just have to work with what you have.

Do you occasionally have to deaden the acoustics in the studio when working on a tile floor?
Sometimes you want to deaden, and sometimes you want to liven. It all depends on the other parts of the room.

How much do you compress the piano signal?
Again, it depends on the piano. There are some pianos that are very peaky. For instance, the Bosendorfer piano is a very self-limited instrument. The treble range above Middle C does not get any louder, whereas some Steinways really get loud up there, so if you want to get a good level for the low part on the Steinway, you’ve got to limit the piano a little bit, or else the high notes just go right through you. The Yamaha electric grand usually does not need to be limited, because it’s got a very self-limited range. If you look at it on a meter, from low note to high note, the high notes actually dip a little bit some of the time, but it’s usually just right. The high notes have more of an apparent level, so you really don’t need more level than that.

How was the piano recorded on Brother to Brother?
There wasn’t any acoustic piano on the album. We used the Yamaha electric grand instead, just because it has a different sound. It’s always nice to go for a new sound, and the Yamaha is good for that, especially when Joe puts his effects on it.

What effects would he use on it?
Oh, it could be anything from a Roland Boss Chorus to a Univibe vibrato unit. It could be an Echoplex or a Korg echo unit, and there are all kinds of equalizers. Joey has got a shitload of stuff, but he always uses the same devices from night to night on a particular song. He would never trust himself if he didn’t have the same hookup.

Do you use any effects when you’re playing the Yamaha?
Oh, no. Basically, we get the EQ from the board on the Yamaha, and I never even have to hear the monitors, because I usually play it during ballads, so I just hear it acoustically onstage.

How do you feel about its tuning stability?
You’ve got to tune it every night. It’s never perfectly in tune, though, especially in the low notes. But, you know, sometimes a detuned piano could have a good sound too. As long as it’s tuned from about maybe an octave and a fifth below Middle C and up, you can handle it. If you’re playing bass notes, you are usually playing octaves, and your thumb is usually playing the note that’s in tune. Maybe your pinkie has got the one that’s a little out, but if it sounds a little wide, sometimes that oscillation is good. And anyway, the tuning is not very apparent when you’re playing in a coliseum or a big concert hall.

On the title cut to Brother to Brother, it sounded like the Yamaha had been intentionally detuned.
Well, we used two pianos there, and one of them had a chorus effect on it. That’s why it sounds highly detuned, but it’s also true that the Yamaha itself had been detuned. In other words, there’s a choral effect on it which detunes the right side signal on your stereo, so the pitch is bending, and that’s why it sounds a little out with itself.

Are you satisfied with the electric grand when it comes to reproducing the sounds of your richly-recorded acoustic pianos?
Well, they’ll probably improve it, but it’s the best electric piano of its sort right now.

Well, since your albums have won Grammys for production quality, has it been hard to match that quality in general onstage?
No, not at all. We’re just completing a live album, and we can’t help but feel that so much of the live stuff is even better than our studio records, even though the live recordings haven’t really been tampered with. We’ve got 24 tracks full of synthesizers, and that’s not any fewer than what we have to deal with in mixing a studio album, so that’s what we’re taking our time with now. What’s taking even more time is finding a song from one night that we like, and wanting to follow it with a song from another night, then trying to join the sounds of the audiences to make it sound like they were done at the same concert. That’s making the going difficult, but it’s working.

Do you have to alter or simplify any of the studio arrangements for live performance?
Sometimes a little bit, but usually not if you’ve got the players.

What criteria did you have for finding those players?
Well, for our current band, we knew that we needed a good left-hand keyboard bass player, because some of the old material features a lot of the bass parts being doubled by synthesizers. It took a little while to find someone who was as good as Brad Cole for that job. This was the first time we’d used Brad. I like his playing so much; I’ll probably use him again in the future. Then there’s Bill Meyers, who plays keyboard bass on a couple of songs at the same time that he’s playing other parts; every hand in our band is usually busy getting the texture that we’re looking for. I mean, you come across good musicians, but they’re hard to find. You won’t necessarily marry them or anything like that, but you keep in mind their abilities, and sometimes you have certain songs that just fit the bill for their abilities.

And this explains why you frequently change the lineup of your group.
You’ve got to change personnel. It’s also a matter of keeping interest up. I find that when you have a band on retainer, and they play your stuff and only your stuff, it could tend to get a little doldrumish after a while. It becomes a fact that the end justifies the means; and whatever it takes to come up with that product, that album, that tour, that sound, that song, you’ve got to go for it.

What instrument is the keyboard bass played on?
Mostly on one of the Korg synthesizers. They came out with a new model that is really dependable. We had tried a few more complex synthesizers for the bass, but it just wasn’t worth the effort.

Do you try to duplicate a bass guitar sound when you double the bass?
No, we didn’t go for a bass guitar sound this time around, on the last tour; we left that up to the bass player. On other tours we played only the list that called for a keyboard bass, so we’d have to emulate a real bass for certain songs, but this time the authentic bass, the bass guitar, was playing, I’d say, two-thirds of the way through the show. Rarely was it not playing, but I should say that a lot of what it was doing was augmented by synthesizer sounds. Many times they’d be playing unison lines.

Why not follow the Gary Wright path and let the synthesizer take over the bass line completely?
Well, I find that if you depend totally on left-hand keyboard bass the sound can get stiff after a while. Obviously we’ve been primarily a keyboard act, but I look at it like I don’t want to confine myself to keyboards or to any other one thing. I love woodwinds, I love brass, I loved stringed instruments, and I love electric stringed instruments. On the next album I intend to use upright bass for a couple of songs, electric bass, synthesizer bass, guitar, some synthesized strings, and maybe some real strings.

Given the number of overdubs of string sounds you did with the monophonic Korg on Gist of the Gemini, you must have been ecstatic when the first polyphonic synthesizers were produced.
I know. My God! It took hours to do one song. The Maxikorg had just two oscillators, and you needed two oscillators to give you some kind of width with the one string sound, so Joe and Richard Baker had to play one note at a time to build up the string section sounds on that album. It’s just not worth it to work that way, because you don’t really know what you have until you’re done mixing it down. There is one advantage to recording one string at a time, though. That’s actually how it’s being done with real string sections. One player is doing one thing, so there is always a separate mind, a separate hand, a separate finger getting the sound from the instrument. That means you have a separate touch, with a little discrepancy in timing, and these personal differences are a part of the sound you get in the end. So in many ways I think you achieve more of what a string section would achieve if you’re playing one note at a time, or if a couple of guys are playing a few notes, because you achieve that subtle imperfection. Whereas with a polyphonic synthesizer, your ten fingers go bam at once on the keys, and there’s no string section that’s ever that perfect. It’s good, but it’s a little bit more plasticene-sounding. It does save a lot of time, though.

It probably keeps the creative momentum rolling too.
Oh, it does. When you’re doing one note at a time, you get tired, your engineer gets tired, everyone gets tired. And when I’m producing on one of those occasions, I’m trying to envision if there’s too much high end on the synthesizer, if the filters are open too much, how it will sound after 28 overdubs: Will it become just a total buzz? Sometimes you’ve done a whole array of overdubs and you realize that the timing is all wrong; once you put them all together, you see that they’re moving in the wrong direction.

Wouldn’t it be easier to hire a real string section instead?
Well, on the next album, we’re going to use both real and synthesized strings. On certain cuts where the strings are not really much more than a blanket or a cushion of sound, it’s not that important to use a real string section, because you don’t really hear those imperfections that make it human. But when you’re doing a ballad, or a song with more of a classical style, it may be wiser to just use a real string section, even though it’s going to cost a lot of money. We’re not just going to hire 15 string players; we’ll probably hire 60 players.

So you see synthesized and real strings as two totally separate musical elements.
They are, but they give you the same effects in many ways. Single notes and solo playing are not really good on synthesizer when you’re going for strings. For instance, when you get a string part like those staccato notes in the Elton John thing, “Philadelphia Freedom,” you should have live strings; the synthesizer isn’t any good in getting you that, in my opinion. It doesn’t sound real; it just sounds fake, too plastic. But I think that when you have a blanket-type sound, like on some of the things we’ve done in the past, it’s very difficult to tell the difference. It’s when you want to have both, like in some parts of “Black And Blue” [from A Pauper In Paradise], when you’re using solo effects and a section comes up playing some lines of the melody with the rest of the instruments providing that blanket of sound, that the true essence of strings comes out.

Has anyone influenced your approach to orchestrating with synthesizers?
No doubt that the best synthesizer orchestrators are Japanese, like Tomita. There’s just no question at this point. There is one other person, Wendy Carlos, whose Switched-On Bach [Columbia, MS-7194 and M-32659] was good, but still Tomita is better. He’s very textural; that’s why he does a lot of pieces by people like Debussy and Stravinsky. But he’s also very precise.

Do you own any synthesizers or dabble around on them in your spare time?
Well, all I’ve got at home is the grand piano, an electric piano, and a set of drums. That’s it. But Joe has a real array of synthesizers sitting in his home, and once in a while he calls me and says, “Well, how do you like this sound? How do you like that sound?” I’ll say, “That’s great. I like this, and I think we could use it for this song,” so it becomes a total cooperative effort.

How do you actually work out the keyboard parts?
Well, basically, the song is written most of the time on my grand piano or on my electric piano at home. I usually have an idea of how it should sound on disc. By the time I get ten or fifteen songs together, we audition players by making them play a few runs that we suspect would be used for those particular songs to see if they would adapt and be useful within the style of the new album or whatever.

Do you write parts out?
No, we just tell the players what to do. If they’re of a certain calibre, you can mumble through your ideas and they’ll be able to pick them up without having them written down. If you have a musician with total uncreativity in his noggin, then you’ll need to write the part. I usually show Joey the changes of my songs first, and then he gets a few musicians together in our rehearsal hall. Then I’ll come up and say, “Let’s try this, let’s try that, and let’s go through the changes.” Certain musicians will take certain notes, perhaps, on various passages to keep from forgetting them, so the only written things you’ll see are some chord charts and maybe some private notes on passages that are hard to play, which the musicians have to take home and practice. But other than that, it’s all verbal.

How are the brass and string parts divvied up?
We use two Korg PS-3300 synthesizers, which each have three separate synthesizer voice modules. You can tune each of the master oscillators to get more realistic chorale effects. Then we have two Korg PS3100s, so all that adds up to about thirty grand worth of synthesizers just to reproduce the string sound onstage. We only use the smaller ones as backup, in case the big ones go. Anyway, what we did was to buy two keyboards and inter-face them into one of the PS3300s, with one keyboard in Bill Meyers’s setup and the other in Brad Cole’s. This way we could switch the string parts back and forth from one to the other as the need arose. The other big Korg was programmed for brass, and the same kind of switching could be done. The synthesizers themselves were kept right beside Joey, so he could tune or fix them if he heard anything wrong. So that’s how we got our string and brass onstage, and they really were incredible sounds, so much so that we’re recording with them right now in the studio, without any overdubs.

Joe Vannelli

What kind of training on keyboard have you and Gino had?
Well, I studied piano privately for about five years and played in various local groups when I was a teenager. It was basically sort of a hobby at the time; I was going to high school and college, and I thought I was going to be an engineer or something like that. I don’t know whether I would have gotten into music by myself, but when Gino was about 15 or 16 he thought that he’d like to pursue a professional career in music. He had studied percussion for about the same amount of time that I had taken piano lessons, and he was a drummer for many years before he decided to get into the singing and writing aspect of music. By the time he was about 16 he was signed to RCA in Canada, but he couldn’t get the exposure and the right push he needed, so he went down to New York and lived there off and on for about two years. By the way, when he was recording up in Canada I would help him out with the sessions, and I did the same thing when he did his demos down in New York. I was sort of commuting back and forth while he was staying there.

Were you playing basically piano then?
Yeah. Gino was doing guitar overdubs while I was doing piano. We hadn’t gotten into the whole synthesized trip yet; that was a whole new area.

What were you playing on your first album for A&M;, Crazy Life?
There were basically two musicians on that: my brother and I. We did all the work on it. He played percussion, and I did all the keyboards. The album apparently didn’t do anything, and we felt that we’d have to go out on the road to get exposure that way. Naturally, two people can’t go out like that and try to create that sound, so we put a band together. Right about that time was when I started looking for different sounds, picking up the synthesizer and getting into it.

What model did you start with?
Oh, just a cheap Univox or Roland, that sort of stuff. I had no idea what it was all about, and I was just slowly fooling around with it at that point in time. At present I’ve got two Korg PS-3300s and two 3100s, plus an Oberheim Eight-Voice and a whole bunch of little synthesizers to put onstage. On top of the fact that we use a Yamaha electric grand and a regular Yamaha acoustic seven-foot grand, we’ve got a Hammond B-3, a Clavinet, a Rhodes, a Wurlitzer… You name it, we’ve got it.

Who plays what keyboard in concert?
Let’s see. In my setup I’ve got a Rhodes, a Wurlitzer, a Yamaha electric grand, an Oberheim Eight-Voice, a Korg K-3, and a Korg MS-20. Bill Meyers uses a B-3 and a Korg synthesizer-he also uses a K-3.

Why use all three electric pianos?
They all have their own inherent sound. I’m really happy they invented the Yamaha electric grand piano, because for once you can really hear the piano player, and it sounds real ballsy compared to a regular piano with just a Helpinstill on it. So naturally we wanted to imitate the acoustic piano onstage. The Rhodes has its own mellow jazzy sound that I like using. I use the Wurlitzer basically for one song right now, “People Gotta Move” [from Powerful People], our old hit.

How are you mixing your keyboards?
Well, all the electric pianos are going through a little six-channel Tapco mixer with three Moog parametric equalizers on each instrument. That’s the sound, those parametrics. I need a lot of EQ, especially on the Rhodes, to get it to sound real bright. I used them on the last album too. I mean, no matter how much EQ you add on the mixer console, you still never get enough top end into the Rhodes. You’ve just got to add a ton of it. I’m running that through one amplifier that I bought in Canada about eight years ago, a GBX amplifier. I’ve got two cabinets with four 12′” full-range speakers in each, and each cabinet is about 150 watts.

What about the synthesizers?
As far as all the synthesizers, we don’t use any amplification onstage. We run them all direct into our 48-channel mixer out front and about 32,000 watts of PA. My brother Ross is mixing the sound that controls all of the synthesizers onstage, so he’s really got to have all the arrangements pretty well down. He creates all of the volume swells and whatever. None of the guys onstage do that; they just bang the keys.

Ross isn’t playing guitar with you, then?
No, Ross doesn’t play onstage as such, although he’s an artist in his own right at this point and he’s pursuing his own career. Hopefully he should be recording soon.

Who is in your group now?
Besides me, there are two other keyboardists onstage; one is Bill Meyers, and the other fellow is Brad Cole. On guitar we’ve got Darryl Stuermer. Then there’s Dave Marotta on bass, Mark Craney on drums-the guy who played on Brother To Brother-two percussionists, two women singers, and Gino out front. We’ve got a new percussionist, a fellow out of Denver named Mike Fisher, a really excellent player. As a matter of fact, all the players in the band are excellent–some of the best players around, actually.

Why three keyboardists?
Our stuff is very orchestrated. It would really be impossible for one guy to do the keyboard parts alone. For example, on a particular tune where I’m doing the comping on the piano and somebody else may be doing the organ and the synthesizer bass at the same time, the third player may be doing strings and brass. Besides, there are too many synthesizers alone to play onstage. I do program the real difficult ones for the other fellows, though. It took me six months just to probe into programming and find out what it could possibly give me. Our band was only put together last January, so a lot of the guys weren’t really familiar with our equipment.

How are the keyboard parts arranged?
When the records are put together we just start off with the nucleus-bass, piano, guitar, and drums, or bass, piano, percussion, and drums, something like that. We begin with the rhythm section and work with that. Then, once that is done, I’ll take the tracks home and try to add lines to them, like string backing or horns. I write out a rough chart for myself, because I know a lot of things are changed at the last minute in the studio. Then we’ll go into the session and start adding all those different sounds. It’s done in stages, actually; it’s not done all at once.

What did you use for string and brass sounds before you got your polyphonic synthesizers?
Oh, we used to kill ourselves! On Gist Of The Gemini we used just a simple little K-3 synthesizer. We had the two 24-track machines set up together, then we used one of them entirely for strings. We had written out the whole arrangement, and we recorded each note one at a time! That meant we had to do something like 65 overdubs. It took us forever. At that time the polyphonic synthesizers weren’t out yet, so everything had to be done individually. That’s how we did it on all the old records, right up until A Pauper In Paradise. When they came out with the polyphonic stuff, we were really happy. It saved us a lot of time, and the results were great also. It really put a strain on our patience to do those overdubs. When you’re in there just listening to one note… [laughs]. I remember Geoff Emmerick, who was our engineer when we were in England recording Gist Of The Gemini, thought we were crazy, but when it all came together it just sounded amazing.

That explains how you got such a fat string sound
Well, there are a lot of overdubs. Naturally, the fat sound usually begins with the drums. If you’ve got a good drum sound, everything else is fairly easy. A synthesizer records real easily. You feed it direct, and it’s there. The acoustic stuff is more difficult to record, and that’s got to be done well. Once you’ve got that, the rest is pretty simple.

How do you record the piano?
On the last albums we’ve used the Yamaha CP-70, but in the past we used an acoustic piano with just two Neumann 47 mikes on it. It’s a lot easier now with the Yamaha. it’s only doubtful on the bass notes, where it’s really difficult to stay in tune. When I play them, I try to stick in the midrange. If a part in the studio would call for specific playing in the low end, then maybe I’d use a regular piano. But with the major portion of what you might play, it works fine.

What kinds of things do you do with the Korg polyphonics?
We can’t do that much with them, since they’re basically programmed and they stay that way. I think there are about a hundred knobs on those synthesizers, and to have to reset them for each tune would just take an eternity. That was the only disappointment I had when I first bought one: I was looking for a computer programmer that could program it, but apparently they don’t have one available yet. I was trying to get one built for me, but there was no guarantee that it would be real stable and dependable onstage, so rather than get ulcers every time you do a concert, I figured we might as well get four or five of the Korgs, have them all programmed differently, and use them that way. Last year, when I went out on the road, I used basically the Oberheim Eight-Voice, and I had problems with the programmer. Every now and then it’d get knocked around, and I’d lose all my programs right before a show. That was panic time!

Have you tried any other programmable synthesizers?
I haven’t really tried anything else, to date. Hopefully I’ll be walking into the stores and talking to people about them soon. Some people have been raving to me about the Prophet 5. I haven’t heard it yet, but I’d like to check it out.

Do you listen to orchestras for ideas of idiomatic string or brass lines to do on synthesizer?
Well, naturally there are certain things that can’t be accomplished with synthesizer. You really can’t get the way a violinist will articulate, because when you try to analyze it there are six or seven or maybe ten different sounds happening at once. The only thing you can get is the layers or blankets of sounds. If you’re trying to create something with a lot of motion to it, you’d have to use a real orchestra. That’s why we did use the Royal Philharmonic for our fifth album [A Pauper In Paradise]. As far as live gigs, though, the synthesizers are really unbeatable, because most of the time, when I check out a live band that has string players, they tend to get lost in the shuffle. You never hear them, whereas with the synthesizer the sound just comes out loud and clear. I can drown the whole orchestra and the whole rhythm section with it. My brother [Ross] has got to be real careful at the board, especially with the 3300, because the PA just sounds enormous.

Have you modified any of your keyboards internally?
As far as any major modification is concerned, no. The only thing we did was, in buying my Rhodes, I tried many of them out, checking them out for action and for overall sound, and when I picked one out, I reset all the notes myself and had the piano padded down a little bit, because the Rhodes tends to overload when you run it too hot. Everything else is basically stock. I just run it all through the EQs to make the sound real punchy and bright and fat.

What effects devices do you use?
We’re not using that many effects. I mean, we use the regular Harmonizer-flanger-DDL-tape echo stuff, mostly Eventide. I think we have a Multivox tape echo. We’ve been lucky with it; we used to use Echoplexes and they were quite noisy.

What about equipment breakdowns? How do you deal with those?
Well, that’s something I don’t like to talk about [laughs]. But we’ve been very fortunate. The only breakdown I ever had was a couple of nights ago, and it was just a bad cable. Everything has held up really well, considering how long we’ve been on the road. You’re always concerned, though, about whether everything will hold up, especially the synthesizers. We’ve got everything heavily cased, and we have pretty conscientious roadies.

So you don’t have any proverbial horror stories to tell?
Horror stories? Oh God, let me think. There was one time when one of our limiters went out, and this excruciating frequency went throughout the whole PA. We use 32 cabinets with two 18s, two 10s, two 2440 JBLS, and two 2205s in each cabinet, and with this one noise I think we destroyed every tweeter in the PA, so we had to do the whole show with no high end. It was torture, just torture. Then you always have the horror story where trucks break down and don’t show up until right before you go onstage. We had that happen to us in Norfolk, Virginia, and in Pittsburgh. The trucks were eight hours late. Now, we won’t go onstage unless we get a sound check. I mean, we have to check every instrument and make sure it’s operational, and to EQ the room itself takes quite a bit of time. We usually have a stage call at nine in the morning, since it takes six or seven hours to set up the rig, but now the trucks arrive at five in the afternoon and nothing is set up. Fortunately, we got at least a ten-minute sound check. That’s the beauty of it. With my kid brother [Ross], he does everything so well that the whole crew was just hustling [laughs].

Speaking of Ross, why is it that you haven’t used many guitar players in the past?
Well, we’ve used guitar players sparingly on the albums. We had a guitar solo in “Mama Coco” and “Where Am I Going?” [both from Storm At Sunup]. We tried to compensate for it live by using the synthesizer. We felt it just wasn’t worth it to carry an extra musician just for those two or three solos. But on the last album we incorporated more guitar playing, and figured it would be worth it to add a guitarist to the band. I guess it was also a question of trying to find the right musician for our concept of how the guitar should be used, and Darryl fit into the concept perfectly. But as far as people talking about us on the road, most reviewers have reiterated that ours is basically a keyboard sound, a thick, blanketed-type sound, with guitar interjected here and there.

How much does Gino have to do with the creation of that sound onstage?
Oh, Gino has a lot to do with it. He writes 90 percent of the music, so he’s got definite ideas about what he wants. He’s a drummer, so he really gives drummers a hard time [laughs]. I mean, he’s got it right down to the different beats that he wants drummers to use. Sometimes he’ll get on the drums and play it for them. He plays keyboards and guitar too, so he knows enough about that to tell people what he wants, but as far as getting into voicings and stuff like that, I have a little bit more knowledge, so I can help him out with that. It’s sort of a family affair. It’s really hard to describe how we all work together; it’s just a culmination of things. One thing he says may spark another thing that I may do, or vice versa.

How exactly do you and he work together on new material?
Well, Gino has the tunes written out, then we’ll get together and go over them, and maybe I’ll tell him that I don’t like this particular line, or I’m not crazy about a particular lick, or whatever. And we just fool around with the songs. We were kicking around some of the songs from the last album for a couple of months. Then, once we get a basic format, we’ll get the musicians together, start working on the basics of the tunes, and build from there.

What influences can you cite with regard to the kind of voicings you might apply to Gino’s songs?
Well, when we were kids we liked the energy and the excitement of rock and roll, but we weren’t crazy about the limited chord structures, the I-IV-V or I-II-V chords. We thought we could add something maybe a little out of the ordinary to rock and roll, to make it special. We grew up listening to the Dave Brubecks and the Oscar Petersons, who were utilizing the kinds of chords we dig years and years ago, and we thought it would be great to combine the musicality of those artists with the energy of rock and roll. And that’s what we’ve been trying to do for the last few years.
item.excerpt:encoded: An interview with Gino and Joe Vannelli as published in the November 1979 issue of Keyboards Magazine.

item.title: Gino Vannelli: A Canadian Musician Of International Stature
item.dc:creator: ava
item.content:encoded:
David Farrell, Canadian Musician Magazine
August, 1979

Standing in the lobby of the Harbour Castle Hilton, he looks like a Florentine bon mot and not far different from that symbol women swoon over on stage. The tightly cut pants, knee high boots and feminine blouse left all too open to expose that tightly curled mass of masculine hair. The peacock composer that the Toronto Sun would chide in its review headline as ‘Mucho Macho … But Not Mucho More’.

Nonetheless, Gino Vannelli is nobody’s servant or slave these days and all matters pertaining to his career are dealt with in utmost seriousness. After 14 years of courting a career in music, it is finally beginning to pay off in dividends and entourage daily grows larger around him, for better or for worse. Today he is quietly stewing over a remark made by the Raes, his opening act in Montreal, who claim their sound was sabotaged at the Forum. “They had equal time for a sound check and we let them use all our equipment including our board,” he counters to a couple of reporters after the damage has already been stated in print.

Twice nominated for a Grammy and recently co-winner of a Juno for excellence in production on the Brother To Brother album, the 27 year-old singer claims many varied influences in his music and remarks that pigeon-holing him into any one style is an unreasonable simplification. Musical osmosis has been a way of life for him since the age of three when he heard his father singing at a dance club in Montreal. Russ Vannelli was, in his time, a local legend who fronted a big band and was once asked to join the Maynard Ferguson band. He declined in favor of settling down with his family, opening up a hair salon and staying home to listen to “the great music” by Coltrane, Bird, Kenton and, later, Brubeck. It was in this environment that brothers Ross, Gino and Joe grew up, at the same time absorbing the Latin and R & B elements that reigned supreme in the city in the late ’50s and ’60s. Early recordings bought by Gino include “Papa’s Got A Brand New Bag” and “In The Midnight Hour” and whilst Joe was toodling around on the piano at home, Gino got to fooling about with a set of second hand drums his parents bought for him. At the tender age of 15 he signed a record contract with RCA, a rather fruitless entanglement that only realized one single, oddly enough under the name Van Elli.

Quickly realizing that RCA had bigger fry to fret over on the label, a meeting was called and release was obtained. Of course the decision was first made over the customary Italian family dinner table where pasta and polemics mixed as freely as the water and the wine. Asked once if these discussions took place while the traditional Italian dishes were being served or after the dishes were cleared? Gino jested “after they were broken.” It was at this point that Gino and Joe decided to try out their musical charm in New York and seek out interest from other record labels. As the story goes, their arrival was the cause of some considerable interest but each query was accompanied by demands on them that neither was willing to acquiesce to and so they returned again to Montreal a little poorer but a great deal wiser.

“That didn’t work out,” recalls the sultry singer who was once billed as Hunk Of The Month by Sixteen magazine. So next came a series of club dates around the city to earn money needed for equipment to set up a basement studio and prepare a demo tape to go out to Los Angeles with. They formed a group called Good Friends and in the course of playing, were booked into Dominic’s where they came to meet Pasquale, a hairdresser of some renown and a close friend of the Vannelli family. As Russ Vannelli and Pasquale both tell the story today, Pasquale was in the club having a drink, saw Gino on stage, then noticed Russ and put two and two together. So taken aback by Gino’s dynamism on stage, he told the parents that someday he intended to do something for them. Meantime, the brothers were socking back performance money and purchased a Sony four-track machine and a primitive synthesizer machine with foot pedals and when they weren’t playing on stage they were in the family rec room rehearsing new material and preparing a demonstration tape. “Basically what we would be doing is setting down a drum track, which was me, then Joey would add some organ, bass pedals and a bit of oscillation and then I would add the vocal at the end. That’s more or less how we came to construct the Crazy Life album.

Initially, they had wanted to use guitar for a demo tape but everytime they approached someone to help out, the subject of money was raised “and frankly we just couldn’t afford any extra expenses, so we started using synthesizer instead. I guess it was the root of evolution.”

Drumming had come naturally to the singer, but it was an early Gene Krupa film that nurtured his desire to sit behind a set of skins to begin with. He joined his first band when he was 12, an aggregation called the Cobras, and then, a year later, Joe and Gino formed their own band, The Jacksonville Five, who played soul music, then the hippest thing for a white band to play. Influences cited include King Curtis, James Brown, and the Bar-Kays. There was also five years of drum lessons and a short stint at the conservatory studying theory, but mostly a lot of slugging it out alone and fooling around with ideas until they jelled.

But back in the basement, circa 1972, expectations were on the rise as the two brothers worked on the material with the four-track machine capturing ideas and sessions for posterity’s sake. Meantime Pasquale was looking for a way to make good on his promise when one evening he was pulling into his usual parking spot at Dominic’s and all of a sudden a limousine carrying Trini Lopez, his Italian arms, and a politician raced for the same spot. Pasquale flew into a mock rage, honking his horn and shouting in Italian, French and English all at the same time. His words were to the effect “If you don’t move this black mother ….”

So the story goes, Pasquale got his parking spot and befriended Trini, telling him about the Vannelli act. The outcome of all this was Trini came out to see the brothers, liked their stuff and told them to look him up if they were ever in Los Angeles. That was all they needed to hear. Six demo tapes later, they were en-route with Pasquale, high in hopes and low in cash. Luckily for them, the record contract with Trini Lopez’ people did not happen for them, but Pasquale hustled feverishly down there and finally got through to Herb Alpert at A&M;: “I tell him back in 1972, ‘Gino’s value to music is what Michelangelo was to art’ and when Gino’s album turn platinum he send me one with inscription – ‘you knew it all the time’.”

Soul Brothers: Seven years and six albums later and things have changed considerably for the family. “There were time when it seemed everything was against us,” remembers Gino with a grin visible on his face today. “When I told A&M; about the War Suite they said that people didn’t want to hear about war, that America had just recovered from Vietnam, but I turned to them and said ‘Look, I have to do it’.”

The motivation behind the extended piece came to him on a sabbatical in Oregon. “I was about 100 miles from nowhere in a cabin and I had this beautiful Yamaha piano in the living room. Every morning I would get up and be amazed at the beauty of my surroundings and then one day I was tinkering with some musical ideas and it dawned on me that there was a lack of appreciation for the natural beauty that I was surrounded by, that it was not always going to be there unless we came to grips with this appreciation. I didn’t want to just write another ecology song and I had already composed the music for the Prelude and Battle Cry.

It suddenly occurred to me that they could be tied together. In a way it is a sort of Shakespearean approach that says it’s not so much a matter of fighting for what one believes in, but more a case of protecting what one has already fought for. It’s not about war, it’s about the lack of love for what we have protected (over the years).”

Following The Gist Of The Gemini, which contained the War Suite, came the Vannelli brothers’ tribute to Gershwin, A Pauper In Paradise. Perhaps the most complex of his recordings yet, the album was recorded in London with the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra with charts done by Don Sebesky.

“We worked together with a small tape recorder: I played the parts I wanted on keyboards and told him where the first movement would begin and end, told him where there should be strings and brass and then he took those ideas and put them down on a chart. We did this in the U.S. then he met me in England. The orchestra was in the studio and we started that morning.

At first I was amazed to hear one of my pieces with 99 musicians, then the reality of the situation got to me and I became a madman running back and forth from the concert hall calling for changes and revisions in the charts. Ultimately I think we got most of it straightened away and that the co-venture made for a very successful piece.”

Both the Gist Of The Gemini and A Pauper In Paradise were, to some degree, experimental works for the singer-composer. Next came the seven months in seclusion, ironing out management problems, pausing to evaluate his career and music and creating time to listen and edit a collection of performance tapes that will be used eventually in a live album situation. The album that was to follow this hiatus was, of course, Brother To Brother and it marked a return to his earlier recordings: the Latin rhythms, simple stories, natural melodies. But it also saw the Vannelli brothers finally add guitar to their battery of electronic instruments.

When the Vannelli brothers first started out, they had to come to arrange material for keyboards and found they really didn’t need to supplement the sound with guitars. Then it became a problem of just how to introduce a guitar, especially when touring and playing older material that used synthesizers in lead parts. By the time the Brother To Brother album came to be released, both Gino and Joe felt comfortable with arrangements for guitar and the decision was made to hire on guitarist Carlos Rios for the sessions. Buoyed by the success of younger brother Ross Vannelli’s songs, I Just Wanna Stop, a North American tour was booked shortly before the new year and rehearsals with the new band began in earnest.

Pasquale figures the recent tour cost somewhere in the region of $750,000 to keep on the road, a convoy that included 41 people on payroll and utilized 4 semi-trailers to haul equipment, lights and the suspended sound system. According to Gino, stage equipment alone included 17 synthesizers, an Oberheim and the guitar, bass and drums. Keyboard gear included four electric pianos, two Rhodes, a Yamaha and Wurlitzer and four polyphonic synthesizers.

The next step in the evolution of the Vannelli brothers is to complete work on a film project that was shot while they were touring, to sell the documentary and then “Who knows where to next,” Gino says throwing his hands in the air. A couple of hours from now and the whole entourage will be somewhere in the U.S. playing before another crowd and hopefully garnering slightly better concert reviews than they did in Toronto. But then these are small points of concern for Pasquale who is still pulling the strings these days. After all, not everyone can see a Michelangelo and recognize it for what it is. He did and he was right, at least in Herb Alpert’s ears he was.
item.excerpt:encoded: An article on Gino Vannelli published in Canadian Music Magazine in August, 1979

item.title: Dream of Gino, Indianapolis
item.dc:creator: ava
item.content:encoded:
K.C., Radio Free Rock, September 1977

Montreal. Home of the hockey Canadians, the 1976 Olympic Games, and one of the most impressive World’s Fairs ever. It is also the birthplace and life-long residence of Gino Vannelli, Italian boy-beautiful, dedicated musician, and one of the most popular curly haired performers since Harpo Marx.

In the city where he once sweated through six hour club gigs, Gino now relaxes between touring and recording sessions. He retreats there for privacy and relaxation, away from the demands placed on the newly famous; for Gino Vannelli is quickly becoming the brightest star to emerge from our northern neighbor since Gordon Lightfoot. This emergence into international prominence is no mere fluke. It is the fulfillment of a dream which began sixteen years ago when nine year old Gino saw his singing father perform, and decided that his goal was also to be a singer. It proved to be more than his goal, It was his destiny.

While other kids dreamed of hockey contracts and firemen’s pensions, Gino and his older brother Joe (later joined by young brother Ross) began experimenting with music. Early jams in the Vannelli household featured Joe on the family piano with Gino pounding out rhythms on pots, pans and cookie jar lids. Vannelli envisioned himself the successor to drummer Gene Kruppa, and was immersed in jazz rather than rock in these early years. (He had five years of drumming lessons.) Gino and Joe soon assembled a crude home recording studio in their family’s basement. It was here that Joe began to learn many of the techniques that he still employs today as Gino’s producer, arranger, keyboardist and all-around right-hand brother. Here too, Gino began to compose his own songs on piano.

By the time Gino was sixteen, he had a contract with RCA and a record in the lofty heights of the Canadian top ten – heady stuff for such a tender, inexperienced lad. Determined not to be a one-shot pop phenomenon, he hit the New York club circuit, eager to acquire experience and recognition in the Big Apple. Alas, he labored virtually unnoticed, although he gained a large cult following.

Gino had already returned to Montreal (to concentrate on writing and composing in familiar surroundings) when he was spotted by Herb Alpert. Convinced that he had discovered something that was begging to be shared, Alpert guided Gino’s first release in 1972. With the issuance of Crazy Lifethe twenty year old artist found himself firmly entrenched on the doorstep of the big time. Although four more LPs and a lot more musicial sophistication have passed beneath the bridge ‘twixt now and then, Crazy Life is still the favorite LP with many of his fans.

With the completion of his second album, Powerful People, Gino’s foot was in the door like a vacuum salesman’s with three mortgages to pay. With nothing more than national exposure need to completely open that door, Gino was soon to be treading the welcome mat. The album produced a single “People Gotta Move”, which found its way onto AM and FM programming charts around the world. (And don’t forget those old Indiana Pacers commercials on Channel 4!)

The disco boom was at that time emerging, and though Gino’s music is far removed from the stereotyped restrictions of the genre, “People Gotta Move” certainly helped spawn the movement. The intensely personal style that embodies Gino’s songwriting began to dominate his music by 1975. His third release, Storm At Sunup, featured many introspective ballads, as well as the upbeat dance number “Mama Coco”, which strengthened Gino’s growing reputation with black and white audiences alike.

In 1976, Gino released Gist Of The Gemini. “I had no secret quest to bare my soul on this album, which drove me to a very emotional state,” Gino has candidly observed about that album. It was this intense, emotional state which further developed his personal lyrical style and his experimentation with complex pieces as an alternative to three minute songs.

The year 1977 was a busy one for Vannelli, with world-wide touring plus recording sessions in London with the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra. These orchestral sessions resulted in two works, “Black And Blue” and “Pauper In Paradise” (the latter in four movements) which comprise side two of his latest album, A Pauper In Paradise.

In late November, with A&M; Records backing him feverishly, Gino embarked on yet another tour. The Vannelli caravan began to encounter the difficulties that develop when a major entourage attempts to travel in the worst weather seen in these parts since … well, since just last winter actually! Among the hardships they endured was a blizzard in Pittsburgh, truck break-downs in Chicago, and food poisoning in Milwaukee — several Midwest dates, including Indianapolis, were rescheduled for March, “in the spring, when the flowers are blooming and everybody feels a bit better.”

On December 12 the tour was nearing holiday break, and Gino had a chance to relax and chat about both recent and not so recent events. Sipping coffee in his sunny suite in the Phoenix (Arizona) Hyatt House, he gave the interview which follows.

Do you ever sit back and wonder if it is really happening, this mass acceptance that is now coming your way?
Well, you see, the mass acceptance has not become full-fledged. I am very happy with the way my career has lead itself; I’m very pleased about the kind of audience I have. It’s an exciting, relatively intelligent, very good music audience, and they make me very happy to perform. I never go on stage saying ‘Oh well, I’ll do this because I know the dummies will like it.’ I always go onstage trying to give them the best — the best sound, the best lights, the best of me, the best of the band — because I know that’s what they are there for. I think the coming thing for music is not going to be the numbers — how many people your playing to — but what kind of people you’re playing to, and that’s very important to me.

Having such deep respect for your audience, do you ever experience stage fright?
All the time. Every time there’s that moment as you get dressed when you finally realize that you’re going out there to perform. I really try to forget about what I’m wearing, how my hair looks or whatever, and just think about singing my best. At that point, I get huge Monarchs floating around in my stomach.

Do you play any instruments in your live show?
Yes, for a couple of songs I dabble a bit on the piano, but that’s about the extent of it. I need to concentrate all my energy on my singing so that I can produce my best vocals.

For many stars, especially virile ones like yourself, fans can become dangerous. Have you ever been afraid of actual physical harm from fans?
A few times … in Chicago, I inadvertently went to touch a few hands and they pulled me into the audience. The second night was even scarier, because — well, we lost count finally — about a hundred girls just sort of leaped up on stage at once, and we just had to make a run for it. Sometimes I go back to my hotel (I always register under an assumed name) and some people who must work for the CIA find out what room I’m in and come banging on my door at six o’clock in the morning. I may get frustrated about that, but overall, if you really want your privacy you can have it. Attention is part of the job, and if you scorn it, you’re defeating your own purpose.

Your music is sensual and suggestive, and often excites the ladies…..
Can you explain that to me?


Well … I think it’s some of the best bedroom music around … I mean, when the sensitivity and warmth of your lyrics and the rhythms of your arrangements are your only contact with much of your audience, then your lyrics become your personality …. the sex symbol syndrome.
I think it’s somewhat of a paradox that it’s going on. The whole sex symbol thing is something that was not premeditated, nor do I think it was contrived. As you said yourself, the lyrics are really just a reflection of my personality. The lyrics are an honest reflection of myself. A lot of people ask me those questions, and they’re really hard to answer. I don’t feel like I’m trying to be a sex symbol. It’s so simple from my end of it … If you spent a week traveling with me, you’d know that there is no big master plan saying, ‘how can we get the women?’ I just go on stage and I sing my songs and I think about my set-up. We;ve spent a lot of money on lighting and sound systems; we just try to put on the best show possible, and all of a sudden these women jump on the stage and are doing these things.
Now, I’m not belittling them in any way. It just happens and we’re actually amazed by it — we smile at it. We don’t expect it. We don’t encourage it. It happens. Maybe it seems premeditated, from the press’ point of view, the outside looking in, but from the inside looking out it’s so simple.

So there is no overt image-building involved?
No. In fact, A&M; has always been pretty much against it. The only people who have really inflated the whole thing are the press, because they usually write about incidents at the concerts and that promotes it further.

The importance of your brother Joe as an influence on your music, through his producing and arranging, is fairly well documented. What about your younger brother Ross?
Ross is a singer-composer also, and he’s been writing songs for a few years. He is very close to our whole music concept and has really contributed a lot.
